pages.t: AI Driven, Human Assisted
pages.h: AI driven, human assisted: the default just inverted
pages.d: For a decade the default was human driven, AI assisted. That order is inverting — and the part left to a person gets harder, not easier. What actually changes.
pages.b: AI Driven, Human Assisted AI practice AI driven, human assisted: the default just inverted For most of the last decade the sensible arrangement was obvious — a person did the work, and a model helped at the edges. That order is flipping. The model holds the plan now and the person holds the veto, and the half left to the human turns out to be the harder half. Here is what actually changed, the four jobs that stay with you, where the inversion is a bad idea, and how I run it in production. Published 21 August 2026 · 12 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The old default, and why it worked Human driven, AI assisted was never a slogan anybody had to argue for. It was simply how the tools worked. Autocomplete finished the line you were already writing. The grammar checker flagged a sentence you had already composed. The model suggested a function body inside a file you had already structured, in a project you had already designed. You held the plan; the tool shaved seconds off the typing. That arrangement was safe for a reason worth naming out loud: the unit of delegation was small enough to check at a glance. If a suggestion was wrong, you saw it the second it appeared, in context, with everything around it still loaded in your head. The cost of a bad suggestion was one keystroke — reject, move on. Nobody ever needed a governance policy for autocomplete. It was also, quietly, a ceiling. A tool that only ever operates one line ahead of you can never save you more than the typing. The thinking, the sequencing, the twenty small decisions between "I need this" and "this works" — all of it stayed with the human, because there was no way to hand any of it over. What actually changed The popular story is that the models got smarter. That is true, and it is not the interesting part. The shift that matters is much narrower: the model started holding the sequence. Give a current system a goal instead of a sentence and it will decompose it, choose tools, run them, read what came back, notice that it was wrong, and try again — for twenty or fifty steps — before it hands you anything at all. That is a different job. It is not writing your next line. It is running the loop you used to run. And once the loop moves, the unit of delegation moves with it. You are no longer accepting a token. You are accepting an outcome , produced by a process you did not watch. The entire safety story of the old arrangement — I'll catch it if it's wrong, because I'm right here — quietly stops bein

pages.t: Automating Email Replies with n8n
pages.d: How I build email reply automations with n8n: the five-stage workflow, where AI helps, guardrails that prevent bad sends, and mistakes to avoid.
pages.b: Automating Email Replies with n8n Automation Automating email replies with n8n Replying to the same kinds of emails over and over is exactly the sort of work software should handle. I've built several of these systems for real clients — including my open-source CleverResponder builds for SmartLead and Instantly. Here's how I structure them, where AI genuinely helps, and the mistakes worth avoiding. Published 18 May 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why n8n for this n8n is a workflow automation tool where you connect building blocks — triggers, logic, and actions — into a flow, without writing a whole application from scratch. For email reply automation it fits well for a few reasons: it talks to email and CRM services out of the box, it lets you drop in custom logic where you need it, and because you can self-host it, sensitive message content doesn't have to pass through a third-party black box. You get the speed of no-code with an escape hatch to real code when a step needs it. The anatomy of a reply-automation workflow However fancy it looks, almost every email automation I build follows the same five-stage skeleton. Understanding this shape matters more than any single node: Trigger — something starts the flow: a new reply lands in an inbox, or a campaign tool like SmartLead or Instantly fires a webhook. Fetch & parse — pull in the message and pull out what matters: sender, subject, body, and any context from a CRM about who this person is. Classify — decide what kind of message this is. Interested? Not interested? A question? Out of office? This is the single most important step, and the one people skip. Draft — generate an appropriate response, often with an AI step guided by a tight prompt and the context you gathered. Act — send the reply, or route it to a human for approval, and log the outcome back to the CRM so nothing falls through the cracks. Every reliable email automation is a variation on this: trigger, gather context, classify, draft, then act — with logging throughout. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. Classify before you generate The temptation with AI is to skip straight to "let the model write a reply to anything." That's how you end up sending a cheerful sales pitch to someone who wrote "please remove me from your list." The fix is to classify intent first , then let each category follow its own path. A reply that clearly says "not interested" should trigger a polite unsubscribe and a CRM update — not an AI-written persuas

pages.t: Character Over Career: Five Choices
pages.h: Character over career: five choices I live by
pages.d: Character over career, satisfaction over success, failure over fear, people over place, goal over gossip — five choices that guide how I live and work.
pages.b: Character Over Career: Five Choices Mindset Character over career: five choices I live by Here is a small habit that runs my life. For a handful of words that start with the same letter, there are two things you could chase. Most people chase one of them. I've learned to chase the other. Same letter, different choice — and the choice makes all the difference. Published 27 July 2026 · 6 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah None of these are original virtues — you've heard all ten words before. What I find useful is the pairing: putting the two side by side forces an actual choice, and the choice reveals what you really value when both options are on the table. Here are the five I keep coming back to. The word on the left is the one I try to choose when both are within reach. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. Character over Career Too many people quietly trade away their moral responsibilities for a paycheck and a better title — the duty they owe their parents, their family, the people who depend on them — because a career seems to demand it. I think that trade is backwards. Character isn't the thing you sacrifice for a career; it's the thing that opens career doors in the first place. Build a reputation for being dependable, honest, and decent, and opportunities come looking for you. A career is what you have; character is who you are while you build it. Careers can be rebuilt after a setback — I've watched people recover from layoffs, failed startups, and false starts. But a reputation for how you treat people, once broken, almost never comes back. I would rather be known as someone you can trust than someone you're impressed by. The impressive fades; the trustworthy compounds. When the two ever pull in different directions, character wins, because it's the only one of the two you actually keep. Satisfaction over Success Success is measured from the outside, and the goalposts never stop moving — there is always a bigger title, a higher number, someone one rung above you. Satisfaction is measured from the inside: did the work mean something, did it help someone, would I do it again. My first paid mentoring session earned me six dollars an hour. By any definition of success, that is nothing. By the measure of satisfaction, it was everything — it told me this work was worth doing, and it pointed my whole path. Chase success and you may never feel like you've arrived. Chase satisfaction and you can be at peace on the way up. Failure over Fear Given the choice

pages.t: Finding the Right Career When Everyone Has an Opinion
pages.h: Finding the right career when everyone has an opinion
pages.d: Follow your passion is bad advice. Here is a more honest method: three things that must overlap, testing instead of deciding, and what to ignore.
pages.b: Finding the Right Career When Everyone Has an Opinion Career & Mentorship Finding the right career when everyone has an opinion I have sat in more than five thousand technical interviews and mentored a lot of people through the first decade of their working life. The single most common thing I hear is not "I cannot get a job." It is "I do not know if this is the right thing to be doing at all." That question deserves a better answer than the one people usually get. Published 27 August 2026 · 8 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why "follow your passion" fails so many people It assumes the passion already exists, fully formed, waiting to be discovered. For a small number of people that is true. For most it is not, and being told otherwise produces a specific kind of misery: the belief that everyone else received a calling and you were skipped. What actually happens for most people is the reverse. Interest follows competence. You get moderately good at something, the work stops being frustrating, you start seeing the interesting problems inside it that were invisible from outside — and somewhere in there it becomes a thing you care about. Passion is far more often a result of getting good at something than the reason you started. If you are waiting to feel certain before you commit, you have the order backwards. Commitment for long enough to become competent is usually what produces the certainty. Three things that have to overlap A career that holds up over decades tends to sit where three things meet. Miss any one and you can predict the failure mode. Something you can become genuinely good at. Not something you are good at today — aptitude at eighteen tells you very little. Something where you improve at a reasonable rate and the improvement is visible to you. Something someone will pay for. This is not a compromise of your ideals, it is the difference between a career and a hobby. Both are worth having. Only one pays rent. Something you can sustain. Not "love every day" — nobody loves every day. Can you do this on an ordinary Tuesday when it is boring, without it costing you your health or the people you care about? Miss one and here is what you get: Good at it and paid, but cannot sustain it — the classic burnout track. Often lucrative right up until it is not. pages.t: Git, Explained From the Object Up
pages.h: Git, explained from the object up
pages.d: Git stops being spells once you know what it stores. The object model, the three trees, what each command actually moves, and the undo toolbox — deeply.
pages.b: Git, Explained From the Object Up Engineering practice Git, explained from the object up Most people use git the way people once used incantations: type this, hope, type it harder. It works until the first merge conflict, the first detached HEAD, the first force-push panic. The cure is not memorising more commands. It is knowing the three things any command can move — because once you can see what git actually stores, every command becomes obvious, including the frightening ones. This week I rewrote 169 commits on this site without changing a byte of content; that is only a sane thing to do if you know exactly what is underneath. Here is what is underneath. Published 29 August 2026 · 12 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The three things git can move Every git command you will ever run manipulates some combination of exactly three places, and the documentation rarely says so out loud. The working tree is the folder you can see — ordinary files, the ones your editor touches. The index (the docs also say "staging area") is git's private draft of your next commit. And the history is a graph of commits, with a handful of named labels pointing into it, one of which — HEAD — marks where you are standing. That is the whole machine. git add copies a file from the working tree into the index. git commit turns the index into a permanent snapshot and moves your branch label forward. git diff compares two of the three places. The commands that frighten people — reset , checkout , rebase — are frightening only because they move more than one of the three at once, silently. Learn the three places and you stop memorising commands; you start predicting them. What a commit actually is Git does not store diffs. It stores snapshots , whole ones, in a content-addressed object store — a small database living in the .git folder. A file's content is stored as a blob . A folder is a tree : a list of names pointing at blobs and other trees. A commit is a tiny text record that points at one tree — the complete state of your project at that moment — plus its parent commit or commits, an author, a date, and a message. Every one of these objects is named by a hash of its own content (SHA-1 in almost every repository you will meet). Change one character of a message and the hash changes, which means the "name" of a commit is its content. Nothing in the store can be edited in place, ever. Git only writes new objects. pages.t: How Cybercrime Cases Are Solved
pages.h: How cybercrime cases are solved: from first alert to the courtroom
pages.d: From first alert to the courtroom: incident response, police investigation, digital forensics, and what makes electronic evidence stand in court.
pages.b: How Cybercrime Cases Are Solved Security How cybercrime cases are solved: from first alert to the courtroom A breach or an online fraud starts two clocks at once — the victim's race to contain the damage, and the investigator's race to preserve the evidence. This is the full lifecycle of a cybercrime case: the incident-response track, the law-enforcement track, the digital forensics where they meet, and the courtroom where it all gets tested. Published 10 August 2026 · 14 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Two clocks start when something breaks The moment a ransomware note appears on a screen, or money leaves an account it shouldn't have, two clocks start ticking. The first is the containment clock : stop the bleeding, get systems back, keep the business alive. The second is the evidence clock : everything you will ever be able to prove about what happened is decaying — logs are rotating, RAM is volatile, and stolen money is hopping between mule accounts. These clocks pull in opposite directions, and most of the damage to a cybercrime case — as opposed to the damage from the crime itself — happens in the first few hours, before any forensic examiner or investigating officer arrives. Not through malice; through reflex. The IT team wipes the infected laptop. The embarrassed victim deletes the chat. The company "handles it quietly" and calls the police three weeks later, when the trail is stone cold. By the time an expert shows up, the case has usually already been strengthened or crippled by people who never realized they were handling evidence. This article walks the whole lifecycle: the victim's track (incident response), the law-enforcement track (complaint to charge sheet), the digital forensics where the two converge, and the admissibility rules that decide what survives in court. The legal specifics are Indian — the portal, the helpline, the statutes — but the discipline underneath is the same everywhere. Track one: the victim side of the case Incident response has a standard shape, and the one most teams borrow is the NIST lifecycle (SP 800-61): preparation , detection and analysis , containment, eradication and recovery , and post-incident activity . Real incidents loop through these phases rather than marching through them. The phase where cases are won or lost is containment — that is where the two clocks collide head-on. pages.h: How I vibe coded this website — and the mechanism that made it hold
pages.d: I described what I wanted, an AI built it, and I kept the authority. The specification, review and gates that turned vibe coding into engineering.
pages.b: How I Vibe Coded This Website Engineering practice How I vibe coded this website — and the mechanism that made it hold I did not hand-write most of this site. I described what I wanted, an AI produced it, and I kept the authority over every decision that mattered. That is the easy half to explain and the wrong half to copy. What actually made it survive is the mechanism I built around the prompting — how I specify, how I verify, and what happens when something breaks. This is that mechanism, with the receipts. Published 21 August 2026 · 11 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah What vibe coding actually got me Let me be honest about the starting point, because the honesty is the useful part. I described pages in plain English and a model wrote them. The first version of this site existed in an afternoon. If you have tried it, you know the feeling — it is genuinely fast, and the output is genuinely fine. It is fine for about a week. The trouble is not that the code is bad. The trouble is that you did not build a system, you accumulated one. Nothing records why the header is structured the way it is. Nothing stops the next change from quietly contradicting the last one. You cannot answer "is this still correct?" because you never wrote down what correct meant. Ask for one more feature and you get one more layer on a foundation nobody documented, including you. This site is 186 pages now — 62 of them browser-based labs that run real language runtimes, 67 games, 27 blog posts, the rest ordinary pages — across more than 160 commits, with zero npm dependencies. Nothing that size survives on vibes. What follows is the scaffolding that let it get there while I was still the one deciding. The prompt is a specification The single biggest change in my output quality had nothing to do with the model. It was realising that a prompt is not a wish. It is a specification, and it should be written like one. "Make the blog look nicer" is a wish. It produces something, you squint at it, you ask again. Three rounds later you have drifted somewhere nobody chose. Compare that with what a real request looks like — the constraints first, the ask second: What a usable spec contains. The goal in one sentence. The constraints that must hold no matter what. The things that must not change. How I will know it worked. And the cases I already know are hard. pages.t: Standing Out in an Internship Interview
pages.h: How to stand out in an internship interview
pages.d: Advice from 5,000+ interviews: why attitude beats aptitude, the homework nobody does, mistakes that sink candidates, and questions worth asking.
pages.b: Standing Out in an Internship Interview Careers How to stand out in an internship interview Between 2021 and 2023, while working at MountBlue and consulting for US firms, I took more than 5,000 interviews. That much time on the other side of the table teaches you what actually separates candidates — and it's rarely what they spent their time preparing. Here's what actually moves the needle, from someone who has done the reviewing at scale. Published 24 June 2026 · 6 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Understand what an internship interview is really for A senior-hire interview asks "can you already do this job?" An internship interview asks a very different question: "will you be worth teaching?" Nobody expects an intern to know everything. What they are actually screening for is coachability, curiosity, and whether you finish what you start. Once you understand that shift, half of interview anxiety disappears — you stop trying to fake expertise you aren't expected to have, and start showing the traits that actually get you picked. Attitude first, aptitude second If those 5,000-plus interviews taught me one thing, it's this: I screen for attitude before aptitude. It sounds backwards — surely skill is what matters? — but the logic is simple. Aptitude can be added. I can teach a framework, a language, a tool; skills are learnable on a timeline. Attitude comes from within, and no amount of training installs it. Curiosity, honesty, the willingness to keep going when something is hard, the instinct to take ownership instead of making excuses — you either bring those to the table or you don't. So a candidate who is a little behind on skills but clearly hungry, coachable, and honest will beat a more polished one who is arrogant or passive nearly every time. What this means for you is freeing: you do not have to walk in as the finished article. You have to walk in as someone obviously worth investing in. Show the attitude, and the aptitude gap stops being disqualifying — it becomes the exact thing the internship exists to close. Do the homework almost nobody does You would be surprised how many candidates can't answer "so, what do you know about my work?" Turning up informed is rare enough that it instantly separates you. Before any interview: Read what the person or company actually does — their projects, their writing, their focus areas — and be able to name one specific thing that interested you and why . pages.t: How to Succeed in Software Development
pages.h: How to succeed in software development: the four-step path
pages.d: Make it work, make it modular, make it readable, then optimize. Why this order is the key to building software and automations that last.
pages.b: How to Succeed in Software Development Craft How to succeed in software development: the four-step path After years of building systems and reviewing thousands of engineers, I've come to trust one simple order of operations. Great software isn't written in one heroic pass — it's grown through four stages: make it work, make it modular, make it readable, then make it optimized. The magic is entirely in doing them in that order. Published 5 June 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why the order matters more than the steps Most people fail at software not because they can't do these four things, but because they do them in the wrong sequence. They optimize before it works. They polish readability on code they're about to throw away. They chase a perfectly modular architecture for a problem they don't understand yet. Each of those is effort spent in the wrong place at the wrong time. The four steps below are valuable precisely because they tell you what to care about now and what to deliberately ignore until later. Each step stands on the one before it. Skip a stair and the ones above it wobble. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. Step 1 — Make it work The first and only job at the start is to get something running end to end, however ugly. One long function, hard-coded values, no error handling worth mentioning — fine. The goal here is not quality; it is proof . A working-but-messy version teaches you what the problem actually is, surfaces the surprises hiding in the requirements, and gives you something real to improve. A beautiful design for the wrong problem is worthless, and you can't know the right problem until something works. The trap at this stage is perfectionism — polishing code you might delete once you understand the problem better. Resist it. Get to working first, and give yourself explicit permission for it to be rough. Step 2 — Make it modular Now that it works, you understand the problem well enough to see its natural seams. Modularity is the step where you break that one big blob into pieces that each do a single job — a function that only parses, a function that only validates, a function that only sends. Good modules have clear boundaries: you can understand one without holding all the others in your head, and you can change one without breaking its neighbors. This matters far more in automation than people expect. A workflow built as one giant tangled step is impossible to debug when it fails at 3 a.m.; the same workflow split int

pages.t: I Open-Sourced My AI SDR
pages.d: CleverResponder is my open-source AI SDR for SmartLead and Instantly: it classifies replies, drafts with AI, gets Slack approval, sends, and follows up.
pages.b: I Open-Sourced My AI SDR Automation I open-sourced my AI SDR Of everything I've automated, this is the build I'm most proud of: CleverResponder, a fully functional AI SDR that handles campaign replies end to end — classify, draft, approve, send, follow up. I built it twice, once for SmartLead and once for Instantly, and both workflows are free on my GitHub. Here's how it works, node by node. Published 3 August 2026 · 6 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The problem: replies are where campaigns go to die Cold outreach tools are great at sending. The trouble starts when someone actually answers. Replies arrive at all hours, in every shape — "interested, send more info", "book me a call", "not interested", out-of-office bounces, and the occasional message that defies categorization. An SDR now has to read each one, figure out what it is, write a response in the company's voice, and follow up if the prospect goes quiet. Response speed matters enormously here, and it's precisely when the team is busiest that replies sit unanswered the longest. That grind is what CleverResponder removes. Not by letting an AI run wild in the inbox — by giving the boring 80% of replies a fast, safe, supervised path, so humans only touch the messages that need them. What it does, end to end Receives every campaign reply through a webhook, the moment it lands. Classifies it — interested, info requested, meeting requested, not interested, out of office, and more. Drafts a reply with AI, grounded in a knowledge document of FAQs and company details — so answers come from your facts, not the model's imagination. Asks a human — the draft lands in Slack with approve/disapprove buttons. Nothing sends without a click. Sends and follows up — approved replies go out; meeting requests get a calendar link, and if no booking happens within a few days, the workflow checks in and nudges. pages.t: India's IT Law, Explained: IT Act to DPDP
pages.h: India's IT law, explained: from the IT Act 2000 to the DPDP era
pages.d: A practitioner's map of India's IT law — the IT Act 2000, Sections 43 to 79, the struck-down 66A, the 2021 Rules, CERT-In directions, BNSS 94, and the DPDP Act.
pages.b: India's IT Law, Explained: IT Act to DPDP Security India's IT law, explained: from the IT Act 2000 to the DPDP era India's digital economy runs on a legal stack most practitioners have never actually read — an e-commerce law from 2000, criminal teeth bolted on in 2008, a thickening rules layer, and now a full data-protection regime. Here is the whole structure in one pass: what each layer says, the folklore worth unlearning, and a reference index you can bookmark. Published 10 August 2026 · Updated 17 August 2026 · 16 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The law stack nobody reads If you build or run anything digital in India, you are already inside this stack: every UPI payment, SaaS security clause, and police complaint quoting Section 66C traces back to a handful of statutes and their rules. Yet most of us meet the law only in fragments, and fragments breed folklore — misquoted sections, invented penalties, a provision struck down a decade ago still cited in complaints. I am not a lawyer — I am a security practitioner who kept meeting these laws in audits, vendor contracts, and incident calls until I read the primary texts. This is the orientation I wish someone had handed me — every claim checked against its primary source and date-stamped where the ground is moving. Not legal advice. This is practitioner orientation — a map of the terrain, not counsel about your situation. For a notice, a summons, an investigation, or a compliance decision, consult a lawyer qualified in Indian law. Verified against primary sources in August 2026; where the law is in flux, I say so. Twenty-five years of Indian IT law in one line — the timeline this article walks. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. The IT Act 2000: why it exists In the late 1990s India had a practical problem: contract and evidence law assumed paper. A "document" was something you could hold; a "signature" meant ink. So when the United Nations adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce (1996) and recommended that member states legislate along its lines, India did. The Information Technology Act, 2000 came into force on 17 October 2000 — the country's first comprehensive law for electronic commerce and computer crime. Its founding achievements sound mundane precisely because they worked: electronic records and digital signatures gained legal validity , so a contract no longer fails merely for being electronic; the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) was created to license the authorities

A single $6 session started more than I realized at the time. Published 19 July 2026 · 9 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The classroom that didn't feel like enough I earned my bachelor's in engineering from a private state college, then a master's focused on information security. On paper that is a clean line. In reality, the classroom always felt like it was describing the world rather than letting me touch it. Lectures could tell me how a system was supposed to behave; they couldn't show me how it broke when someone poked it the wrong way. That gap — between knowing about something and having actually done it — is the thing that has shaped every decision since. So I started building and breaking things on my own machine. Most of it went nowhere. But one of those late-night rabbit holes turned into the first real milestone of my career. The paper I almost didn't write I got curious about a deceptively simple attack: the fork bomb. A tiny snippet that tells a system to endlessly copy itself until it grinds to a halt. What fascinated me was that even a properly hardened Linux machine could be brought down by it, because creating a process is a completely ordinary thing that needs no special permission. The existing defenses all had a catch — they either blocked legitimate work or punished innocent programs forever. I thought I had an idea for something better, and I nearly talked myself out of writing it up. Who was I to publish? A student. But I did the work, ran the experiments, and it became a peer-reviewed paper — Security Against Fork Bomb Attack in Linux Based Systems , published in IJRAT. It earned a silver medal from Shantilal Shah Government Engineering College and IPCL, and was nominated for a best-paper award by the International Association of Engineers (IAENG). The lesson wasn't "I'm brilliant." It was that the gap between an idea and a published result is mostly just the willingness to actually finish. pages.d: Why your password is rarely the weak point, what a passkey actually is, what it fixes, what it does not, and a setup you can finish this week.
pages.b: Passwords, Passkeys, and What Actually Protects You Security Passwords, passkeys, and what actually protects you Almost nobody loses an account because somebody guessed their password. They lose it because the same password was used somewhere that got breached, or because they typed it into a page that looked right and was not. Understanding which threat is which is the difference between security advice that helps and security advice that just makes your life harder. Published 27 August 2026 · 9 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah How accounts are actually lost There are four common routes, and they are not equally likely. Ranked roughly by how often they land: Reuse after somebody else's breach. A site you signed up to years ago is compromised, and the email-and-password pair from it gets replayed against your bank, your mail, your everything. This is credential stuffing , and it requires no cracking at all — the password is already correct. You can check whether a password of yours appears in known breach data using the breach checker , which does it by k-anonymity so the password never leaves your browser. Phishing. You are sent somewhere convincing and you type the password in yourself. No technical weakness in your password is involved. A long random one is phished exactly as easily as a short one. Pull a suspicious link apart before you visit it and you will see how much a URL can hide. Offline cracking after a breach. If the breached site stored passwords badly, attackers grind through them. How long that takes depends almost entirely on the site's choices, not yours — billions of guesses per second against MD5 , a few thousand against bcrypt . You can watch that difference happen in the hash cracker . Actual online guessing. Rare, because every serious service rate-limits it. This is the threat most password advice is written for, and it is the one that matters least. Three of those four are unaffected by how clever your password is. That is the whole reason the industry is moving on. What still matters about passwords Two things, and only two. Length, not decoration. Substituting 3 for e adds essentially nothing — cracking tools have known that trick for decades. Adding words adds real entropy . Four unrelated words beat P@ssw0rd! by an enormous margin and are far easier to type. Measure it rather than guess : the difference is not subtle. Never reusing them. pages.h: Scope the work before you quote it
pages.d: Most bad projects are not underpriced, they are under-scoped. Five questions to answer before you send a number, and how to change scope without resentment.
pages.b: Scope the Work Before You Quote It Business Scope the work before you quote it Nearly every project I have watched go wrong went wrong in the same place, and it was not the price. It was the sentence that said what the work was — because there wasn't one. Scope is not paperwork you do after winning the job. It is the thing you are actually selling, and writing it down is the cheapest insurance either side will ever buy. Published 27 August 2026 · 7 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Under-priced and under-defined are not the same problem When a project loses money, the reflex is to conclude you charged too little. Sometimes that is true. Far more often the rate was fine and the boundary was missing — so the work kept growing while the number stayed still. Doubling your rate does not fix that. It just means you lose more slowly on a job that has no edges. You can tell the two apart with one question: if the work had stopped where you both originally imagined, would the price have been fair? If yes, you did not have a pricing problem. You had a definition problem. A scope is not a list of tasks. It is a description of the edge — what is inside, what is outside, and what has to be true for the inside to be possible. The five questions to answer before you send a number None of these are clever. They are simply the five things that, when left unanswered, later turn into an argument. Answer them in writing, in the client's own words where you can, and most of the argument never happens. 1. What does "done" look like, observably? Not "improve the onboarding flow" — that has no end. "A new user can sign up, verify their email, and reach the dashboard without support contact." That has an end, and both of you can see it from across the room. 2. What is explicitly not included? This is the sentence people skip because it feels negative, and it is the single highest-value line in the document. If you are hardening a web application, say plainly that it does not cover the mail server, the staff laptops, or the third-party plugin they bought last year. 3. What do you need from them, and by when? Access, credentials, a decision-maker, sample data, a staging environment. Most delays that get blamed on the contractor were actually a week spent waiting for a login. Name the dependency and name the date. 4. How many rounds of revision? "Until you're happy" is not a scope, it is an open tab. Two rounds is normal and generous. Say two. 5. What happens when something changes? Ans

Sort the seven that way — with the requirements that matter in practice — and it becomes obvious which are obligations, which are choices, and which are actually yours. Published 10 August 2026 · 12 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Compliance is trust made auditable Every security consulting conversation I have eventually lands on the same question. Not "how do we stop attackers" — that one comes with the territory — but some version of: "GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2, ISO-something… which of these actually apply to us?" It comes from founders, engineering leads, and operations people holding a 300-question vendor questionnaire — always in the same slightly exhausted tone. It's a fair question, because the alphabet soup hides a real distinction: these frameworks are not the same kind of thing. Some are laws, with regulators and fines behind them. One is a contract you accepted the day you started taking card payments. Some are voluntary standards you can certify against, and one is an accountant's opinion about you. Mix those categories up and you get the classic failure mode I keep meeting: a company proudly chasing a certificate it doesn't need while ignoring a law that already applies to it. Here is the framing that unlocks all of it: compliance is trust made auditable. Every framework below turns "trust us with your data" into something a third party can verify. And every one of them is a floor, not a ceiling — the minimum a regulator, bank, or customer will accept, not a level attackers find inconvenient. The attack families I mapped in the previous post do not check your certification status before firing. The lay of the land: seven frameworks in one table Before the deep dives, orientation. The most useful column is the second one — what kind of thing is this? — because it tells you who enforces the framework and what actually happens when you fall short. pages.h: Smart feedback: how to give and receive it
pages.d: Why vague praise fails, a three-part structure for feedback that actually helps, and how to receive criticism without getting defensive.
pages.b: Smart Feedback: How to Give and Receive Mentorship Smart feedback: how to give and receive it Feedback is the engine of growth, and most of it is wasted — too vague to act on, too harsh to hear, or too polite to matter. After years of mentoring, here is how I try to give feedback that actually helps, and how to take it without your defenses swallowing the lesson. Published 15 June 2026 · 4 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why most feedback does nothing "Good job." "This could be better." "I didn't love it." These feel like feedback, but they change nothing, because the person receiving them has no idea what to actually do differently. Vague praise is pleasant and useless. Vague criticism is unpleasant and useless. Both fail for the same reason: they describe a feeling instead of pointing at a specific, changeable thing. Useful feedback is specific, actionable, and kind — and the order matters. Specific so the person knows exactly what you mean. Actionable so they know what to do next. Kind so they can actually hear it instead of bracing against it. Miss any one of those and the feedback simply gets ignored, no matter how right you were. A simple structure I keep coming back to When I give feedback, I try to hit three beats in order. It stops me from being vague and keeps the conversation forward-looking: Observation — the specific thing I noticed, stated as a fact, not a judgment. "This function does four different things" rather than "this is messy." Impact — why it matters. "That makes it hard to test, and harder for the next person to change safely." Path forward — a concrete next step, ideally as a question. "What if each responsibility became its own small function — how would you split it?" The order matters. Lead with the observation so it's grounded, explain the impact so it's motivated, and end on the path forward so the person leaves with momentum instead of a wound. Observation grounds it, impact motivates it, and the path forward turns criticism into a next step. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. Praise deserves the same rigor We obsess over how to deliver criticism and get lazy with praise — but "great work" is just as empty as "needs work." If someone did something really well, tell them exactly what, so they can do it again on purpose. "The way you named these variables made the whole thing readable in one pass" teaches a repeatable skill. "Nice" teaches nothing. pages.h: The four M's every business runs on
pages.d: Manpower, money, mind, and management: what each pillar means, why businesses fail when one is missing, and how management binds the rest.
pages.b: The Four M's Every Business Runs On Business The four M's every business runs on Strip any company down to its foundations and you find the same four pillars holding it up: manpower, money, mind, and management. Every business has all four, whether the founder names them or not — and the moment any one of them cracks, the whole structure starts to lean. Here's what each really means, and why management is the one that holds the rest together. Published 10 July 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah I've seen businesses from a lot of angles — as a consultant building systems for them, as someone who has interviewed thousands of the people who staff them, and as someone running a small operation of my own. Across all of it, the same pattern holds: a company is a structure resting on four M's. Three of them are the resources; the fourth is what turns those resources into results. Manpower, money, and mind are the pillars. Management is the foundation and beam that keeps them working together instead of apart. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. 1. Manpower — the people who do the work Nothing gets built without people, and a business is only ever as strong as the people inside it. This is the pillar I know best, because I've spent thousands of interviews trying to judge it. The lesson from all those conversations is the one I keep repeating: hire for attitude first, aptitude second. Skills can be taught; character, curiosity, and ownership have to be there already. But manpower isn't just hiring — it's keeping good people and getting the best from them. A team of brilliant individuals who don't trust each other will lose to an average team that does. Culture, motivation, and how people are treated aren't soft extras; they're the difference between a workforce that carries the business and one that quietly drags it. 2. Money power — the fuel Money is the fuel every other pillar burns. You need it to pay people, to buy tools, to survive the long stretch before a good idea starts paying for itself. Plenty of promising businesses with great teams and great ideas still died simply because they ran out of runway before they got there. Cash flow, not profit on paper, is what actually keeps the lights on. But money is only fuel — it isn't the engine. Capital alone builds nothing; it just buys you time and options. I've watched well-funded efforts waste every advantage because money covered up problems it should have exposed. Respect money enough to manage it car

pages.t: The Life of the Buddha, Without the Mythology
pages.h: The life of the Buddha, without the mythology
pages.d: Who Siddhattha Gotama actually was, what the earliest texts say, where the familiar legend was added later, and what he taught in forty-five years of walking.
pages.b: The Life of the Buddha, Without the Mythology Life The life of the Buddha, without the mythology Almost everything most of us know about the Buddha arrived through a long chain of retellings, and a good deal of it was added centuries after he died. That does not make the story less interesting — it makes it more so, because underneath the gold leaf there is a person who lived, taught for forty-five years, and was unusually insistent that nobody take his word for anything. Published 27 August 2026 · 10 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah What we can actually say about him He was born Siddhattha Gotama — Siddhārtha Gautama in Sanskrit — into the Śākya people, in or near Lumbini in what is now Nepal. His father, Suddhodana, led the clan. The Śākyas were a small oligarchic republic rather than a kingdom, which already sits awkwardly with the "prince in a palace" image. Even his dates are unsettled. Traditional reckoning gives roughly 563–483 BCE; a good deal of modern scholarship prefers a later window, closer to 480–400 BCE. A century of uncertainty about someone this significant is a useful reminder of how thin the ground is. What we have is the Pali Canon, written down in Sri Lanka around the first century BCE after generations of careful oral transmission, along with parallel collections preserved in Chinese and Sanskrit. Where those independent lines agree, we are on reasonably firm ground. Where a story appears only in later commentary, it is later commentary — which is not the same as false, but is worth knowing. The four sights, and where they come from The famous version: a sheltered prince, kept from all suffering, ventures out and encounters an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic — and leaves that night. It is a superb piece of storytelling, and in that fully-developed form it belongs to later biographical literature, principally the Nidānakathā commentary, composed many centuries after his death. The earliest texts are quieter and, to my ear, more affecting. In one discourse he simply describes noticing that he was himself subject to ageing, sickness and death, and that this made his own comfort feel hollow. There is no dramatic outing. There is a young man of some privilege who registers a fact everybody knows and is unable to un-notice it. The legend has him shocked by the discovery of suffering. The early texts have him disturbed by the ordinary fact of it — which is a thing that can happen to anyone, on any afternoon. Six years of

pages.t: The Resume-Builder Paywall Trick
pages.d: Resume builders show the price only at the download button. Where the work history you typed actually goes, and why the print dialog is the free export.
pages.b: The Resume-Builder Paywall Trick Security The resume-builder paywall trick The editor looks free right up until your entire work history is typed into it — then the price appears, at the download button, after the sunk cost and never before it. This is how that funnel works from the inside, what actually happens to the data you typed, and why the export button has been sitting in your browser, free, the whole time. Published 22 August 2026 · Updated 27 August 2026 · 6 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah How the trick is staged Search for a resume builder and the top results all open the same way: a clean editor, a row of templates, a live preview, and no price anywhere on the page. You pick a template and start typing. Name, phone, email, city. Every employer you've had, with dates. Education. Skills. Thirty to sixty minutes of honest work, and the preview looks genuinely good — that part is real, the editors are usually well built. Then you click Download , and the product reveals itself. First a sign-up wall — the document you just wrote is held behind an account. Then the actual mechanism, which comes in two flavours: a PDF with a watermark across your work history, or a checkout page. Often the checkout is a "trial" for a small amount that quietly renews at a much larger monthly rate, with the cancellation path buried somewhere in an account settings page you will visit exactly once, angry, three months from now. The price was never missing. It was scheduled — for the exact moment your cost of walking away is highest. That timing is the whole design. Before you typed anything, the honest comparison was "this site versus any other site." After an hour of data entry it is "pay a few hundred rupees versus retype everything somewhere else," and the sunk cost does the selling. None of this is illegal — the terms are disclosed, technically, somewhere — but it is a textbook dark pattern: the interface is engineered so you commit before you can evaluate. Each step raises your cost of leaving. The price is revealed only at the last one, which is not an accident. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. Where your work history goes The paywall is the visible half of the business. The quieter half is what you typed. A live preview means every keystroke is application state, and on most builders that state autosaves to their servers — that is how the sign-up wall can promise your document will "still be here" when you come back. pages.h: Types of cyberattacks, mapped: causes, defenses, and the CIA triad
pages.d: A practical map of cyberattack types — social engineering, malware, network, DoS, web, and credential attacks — with causes, prevention, and the CIA triad.
pages.b: Types of Cyberattacks & the CIA Triad Security Types of cyberattacks, mapped: causes, defenses, and the CIA triad Every attack you have ever read about — phishing, ransomware, DDoS, SQL injection — breaks one of just three promises a system makes. This is the map I wish someone had drawn for me: six attack families, why each one keeps working, and where prevention ends and mitigation begins. Published 10 August 2026 · 13 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The three promises every attack breaks Security has a reputation for being endless — new attack names every week, each sounding like its own specialty. But underneath the naming noise, every attack is trying to break one of exactly three promises. Security professionals call them the CIA triad : Confidentiality — only the right people can see the data. Broken when secrets leak: stolen customer records, read email, exposed credentials. Integrity — the data and the system are what they claim to be. Broken when something is altered: a tampered invoice, a poisoned software update, a defaced site. Availability — the system works when legitimate users need it. Broken when service stops: a flooded server, an encrypted disk, a frozen machine. This lens is the whole trick. Ask "which promise does this attack break?" and an unfamiliar attack stops being scary vocabulary and becomes a variation of something you already understand. Ransomware is primarily an availability attack that uses malware. Phishing is usually a confidentiality attack that goes through a person instead of a computer. My own research subject — the humble fork bomb — is a pure availability attack made of nothing but permitted actions. Attackers don't respect category boundaries, and real incidents chain several types together. The categories aren't for the attacker's benefit — they're for yours, because each family falls to the same kinds of defense. The map: six attack families Here is the landscape in one picture. Six families, grouped by how the attack works — through people, code, networks, load, applications, or logins — with the promise each one usually breaks. Six families, organized by how the attack travels — and badged with the CIA promise each one most often breaks. Real incidents chain families together. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. pages.t: Types of Love, and Choosing Someone to Marry
pages.h: Types of love, and choosing someone to marry
pages.d: The different things we call love, telling infatuation from the real thing, what predicts a lasting marriage, and the questions to ask before you commit.
pages.b: Types of Love, and Choosing Someone to Marry Life Types of love, and choosing someone to marry English gives us one word for the feeling you have about your mother, your closest friend, someone you met three weeks ago, and a plate of food. That is a genuine handicap, because the most consequential decision most people make hinges on telling those apart. This is what I have found useful — offered as one person's thinking, not as instruction. Published 27 August 2026 · 11 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah One word doing too many jobs Greek is often held up as having solved this with a neat set of words for different loves. That is partly true and partly a modern tidying-up — the ancient usage was messier than the lists suggest, and the popular "six types" framing owes a lot to the psychologist John Alan Lee, writing in the 1970s. Still, the distinctions are genuinely useful, whatever their provenance: Eros — desire and passion. Intense, physical, and by its nature not constant. Philia — deep friendship. Respect, shared interests, enjoying someone's company for its own sake. Storge — the steady affection of family. Unglamorous, and it survives things the others do not. Pragma — a settled, practical love built over long partnership. Compromise, patience, shared logistics. Agape — love that expects nothing back. Philautia — regard for yourself. Healthy in one form, corrosive in another. The practical point: a marriage that lasts usually needs at least three of these running at once, and the one that gets all the attention in films — eros — is the one least able to hold weight on its own. Infatuation and love are not the same thing Infatuation is not a lesser love. It is a different state, with a different chemistry and a different time course, and mistaking one for the other is the origin of a great many bad decisions. Some honest tests: Is it about them, or about how you feel around them? Infatuation is largely about your own state. If you strip out the excitement, is there a person left you actually admire? Can you describe their flaws without flinching? Infatuation edits them out. Love has seen them clearly and stayed anyway. If you cannot name three real ones, you do not know them yet. How is it when nothing is happening? Anyone is pleasant on a good evening. Are you comfortable together doing something boring? What does it do to your other relationships? pages.h: What sixty-six tiny games taught me about serious software
pages.d: Sixty-six browser games held every production bug class in miniature — state machines, shared keyboards, saved dead ends, dishonest copy. What each one taught.
pages.b: What 66 Games Taught Me About Software Engineering practice What sixty-six tiny games taught me about serious software The games page on this site looks like a break from the serious work. It turned out to be the serious work in miniature. Across sixty-six small games, every class of bug that matters in production showed up somewhere — inputs, state, persistence, promises — each one small enough to see whole and cheap enough to learn from. This is what they taught, with the receipts. Published 29 August 2026 · 10 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why a security site ships Pac-Man The games section shipped with sixty-six of them — Pac-Man and Tetris remakes, chess against three strengths of engine, seventeen terminal toys including one that does nothing but grow a bonsai tree. No ads, no accounts, nothing to install. A fair question is what any of that is doing on a consultant's website. Part of the answer is that nine of them are security games. One deals you twenty emails and texts, half of them genuine, and makes you call each one — phishing practice with the reason given the moment you answer. Another lets you type a password and watch a real cracking run go after it: wordlist first, then mangling rules, then brute force . People who will not read a paragraph about password hygiene will happily lose to that game three times in a row, and the lesson survives in a way the paragraph never does. Play is the oldest teaching technology there is. But the honest answer is the other one: building the games taught me more than building the serious pages did. A game is ordinary software with the difficulty turned up — real-time input, persistent state, an impatient user — and none of the forgiveness. Nobody files a bug report against a marketing page. Everyone notices when Pac-Man eats a ghost he has no right to eat. Every bug in this article is real. Each one shipped, was caught by the adversarial review this site's build depends on, and is fixed now. What makes them worth writing about is that none of them is really a game bug. Each is a production bug class, caught small. A game is a state machine wearing a costume Strip the pixels off any of the sixty-six and the same skeleton is underneath: ready, playing, paused, game over. Four states, a handful of legal transitions, and every input the player can produce has to mean something sensible in all four. The bug that taught me this had a nasty shape. pages.t: What a Marriage Biodata Leaks
pages.d: One A4 marriage biodata carries birth details, mother's name, address, income and a photo that may embed GPS — read it like an attacker before you share it.
pages.b: What a Marriage Biodata Leaks Security What a marriage biodata leaks No other document an Indian family shares as casually carries as much identity as a marriage biodata: date and place of birth, mother's name, home address, income, and a photograph — one A4 page, forwarded to people you have never met. This is that page read the way an attacker reads it, and the sharing hygiene that costs nothing. Published 22 August 2026 · Updated 27 August 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah One page, read as an attacker reads it Lay a typical biodata on the table and inventory it the way you would audit a system. Full legal name. Date of birth — and usually the time and place of birth too, because horoscope matching wants them. Father's full name, mother's full name. The complete home address. Height, and the education line. Employer, designation, and an income figure stated to the rupee. Sibling names and what they do. A phone number, and a photograph, usually taken at home on a phone. I recently wrote about what resume builders do with your work history , and a resume is genuinely the milder sibling of this document. A resume tells a stranger where you worked. A biodata tells them who your mother is, where you sleep, what you earn, and when and where you were born — and then it gets forwarded through WhatsApp groups and matrimonial brokers to an audience nobody is keeping a list of. The document is not the problem; the fact that nobody treats it as sensitive is. Half the page is account-recovery answers Look at the classic identity-verification questions still used by banks, telecom operators, and older account-recovery flows: date of birth, place of birth, mother's maiden name. Now look at the biodata again — it answers all three, in print, above a photograph. Security people call this knowledge-based authentication, and it fails precisely when the "knowledge" has been shared; a biodata shares it with every household and broker in the chain. The same fields are the skeleton of a convincing "verification call." A caller who opens with your full name, date of birth, father's name, and address does not sound like a stranger — and that credibility is the raw material for SIM-swap attempts and bank social engineering. None of this means a biodata causes identity theft. It means the page is a pre-filled answer sheet, and the only remaining question is who ends up holding a copy. Treat a biodata the way you would treat a photocopy of your passport: fine to show, worth

pages.t: What Happens After We Die
pages.d: What the major traditions actually claim about death, where they disagree, what near-death experiences do and do not show, and living with an open question.
pages.b: What Happens After We Die Life What happens after we die This is the one question every tradition has taken a position on and none has settled. I am not going to pretend to an answer. What I can do is set out honestly what the main views actually claim — including where they contradict each other in ways that usually get glossed over — and what the evidence does and does not support. Published 27 August 2026 · 10 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why the question will not go away Every human culture we know of has developed elaborate beliefs and rituals around death. That universality is sometimes offered as evidence that something is there, and sometimes as evidence that we are simply built to find the alternative unbearable. Both readings are available and neither is decisive. What is certain is that the question is not idle. How you answer it shapes how you spend a life — what you fear, what you are willing to endure, what you consider worth doing. It deserves better than either confident dismissal or confident assertion. What happens to the body This part is not disputed. Circulation stops, oxygen delivery to tissue ends, and cells begin to fail — neurons within minutes, other tissues over hours. Electrical activity in the brain ceases. Decomposition begins. The disagreement is entirely about whether that is a description of the whole event or only of its physical component. Everything below turns on that single question. The materialist answer On this view, consciousness is something the brain does , in the way digestion is something the stomach does. When the organ stops, the process stops. There is no one left to experience absence, so there is nothing it is like to be dead. The supporting evidence is real and cumulative: damage to specific brain regions reliably alters specific aspects of personality, memory and perception. Anaesthesia interrupts experience entirely. Nothing we have found so far requires anything beyond the physical to explain. The honest gap is that we do not have an account of why physical processes produce subjective experience at all — the "hard problem". That is a genuine open question in philosophy of mind. It is not, by itself, evidence for survival, but anyone claiming the matter is fully closed is overstating. Rebirth: two views that are not the same These get flattened together constantly, including in India where both are ambient. They differ on the point that matters most. pages.t: What Is a Fork Bomb in Linux?
pages.h: What is a fork bomb, and why can it freeze a Linux system?
pages.d: How one line of Bash can freeze a hardened Linux system, why ulimit and blacklists fall short, and the smarter defense from my research.
pages.b: What Is a Fork Bomb in Linux? Linux security What is a fork bomb, and why can it freeze a Linux system? One short line of Bash can bring a healthy Linux machine to its knees — no exploit, no special privileges, nothing that looks like an attack. This is how it works, why the usual defenses aren't enough, and the approach I proposed in my research to handle it more gracefully. Published 27 May 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Run it yourself, safely. There is a real Linux machine on this site that boots inside your browser with a hard 64 MB ceiling. A fork bomb in there does exactly what this article describes and costs you nothing but a reboot. One catch worth knowing: that shell is BusyBox ash , which rejects the famous :(){ :|:& };: with bad function name — use f(){ f|f& };f instead. Same bomb, one character of difference. Open the Linux terminal The one-liner that does the damage The classic Bash fork bomb is famous for how little it takes: Warning — do not run this. Pasting this into a shell will freeze your machine almost instantly, even inside many VMs, and you'll need a hard reboot. Read on to understand it instead. :(){ :|:& };: It defines a function called : that calls itself twice and pipes one copy into the other, running both in the background — then invokes it. Each process immediately creates two more, which each create two more, and so on. There is no upper limit written anywhere. It is exponential growth with no brake pedal. The unsettling part isn't the cleverness of the code. It's that every individual action it takes is completely legitimate. Creating a process is something any user is allowed to do. Why "just one more process" ends the system Every running program on Linux is a process, and the kernel tracks each one in a finite structure called the process table. Processes also consume memory and CPU scheduling slots. A fork bomb doesn't break any single one of these — it exhausts all of them at once. The process table fills, memory runs out, and the scheduler is so busy juggling a flood of near-identical processes that legitimate work never gets a turn. The result is a machine that hasn't crashed and hasn't been hacked in any traditional sense — it is simply too busy multiplying to respond to you. In security terms, this is an attack on availability , one of the three pillars of information security alongside confidentiality and integrity. pages.t: Lessons from Running an Internship Cohort
pages.h: What running an internship cohort is teaching me about mentorship
pages.d: Why small cohorts beat crowds, hiring for hunger over resumes, giving real work instead of exercises, and why mentorship is mostly restraint.
pages.b: Lessons from Running an Internship Cohort Mentorship What running an internship cohort is teaching me about mentorship When I started mentoring, I assumed the hard part would be teaching. It wasn't. The hard part was everything around the teaching — picking the right people, designing work that actually matters, and learning when to step back. Most of these lessons come from years of mentoring interns and engineers; running my own cohort now is testing every one of them. Published 2 July 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah A crowd is not a cohort The first thing I got wrong was thinking bigger was better. More applicants felt like success. But a mentorship group is not an audience — it is a working team, and teams have a size beyond which the magic disappears. Past a handful of people you stop mentoring individuals and start broadcasting to a room. Questions go unanswered, quieter people vanish, and the whole thing flattens into a lecture. So I keep my free cohort deliberately small — two or three seats. Not because demand is low, but because attention is finite. I would rather change three careers than entertain thirty inboxes. Small enough that I remember what each person is stuck on without checking my notes; that is the right size. Select for hunger, not résumé Early on I over-weighted credentials — grades, the name of the college, a long list of courses. It is the easiest thing to sort on and almost the least useful. Across the interns and mentees I have mentored over the years — and now in my own cohort — the ones who grew fastest were rarely the ones with the shiniest CVs. They were the ones who showed up with a half-broken project they had built on their own, because that told me the one thing a transcript never can: they will do the work when nobody is watching. Now I look for three signals — evidence they have built something unprompted, the ability to describe a problem clearly, and honesty about what they don't yet know. Someone who admits "I haven't learned this yet" and then tells me how they plan to learn it is worth more to me than any confident bluffer. The goal of selection isn't to reward the best past — it's to find the people most likely to do the work now. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. pages.d: Which AI tool fits which job — chat, research, slides, video, code, automation. What each is good at, what the free tier gives you, and where free stops.
pages.b: Which AI Tool for Which Job AI tools Which AI tool for which job Nobody actually wants "the best AI tool." They want the right tool for one specific job — a deck by Thursday, a research summary, a voiceover, a workflow that stops the copy-paste. So this is organised by job, not by brand. For each one: what it's genuinely good at, what the free tier gives you, and the exact point where free stops being enough. Published 7 August 2026 · 18 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah On prices and limits. Everything below was checked in August 2026. This category moves faster than any blog can keep up with — plans get renamed, free quotas get cut, and new tiers appear every few weeks. Treat the numbers here as the shape of the market, not a quote. Always confirm on the vendor's own pricing page before you pay. Start with the job, not the tool The reason most "best AI tools" lists are useless is that they answer a question nobody asked. You don't have a tool problem. You have a Thursday problem: a deck to build, a hundred emails to triage, a paper to understand, a client demo to record. The tool is downstream of that. So before you open a single pricing page, answer three questions. What is the actual output? A file, a decision, a saved hour? How often does this job come back? Once, or every week? What happens if the output is wrong? A typo you fix, or an email your client reads? Those three answers pick your tool faster than any comparison table, because they tell you whether you need a generalist, a specialist, or an automation — and whether a free tier can carry it. A one-off job that fails harmlessly? Use a free generalist. A weekly job with real stakes? Pay for the specialist. A job that repeats a hundred times a month? Stop shopping for tools and build a workflow. That last one is most of what I do for clients, and it's usually the cheapest answer of the three. The frequency question does most of the work. Most people over-buy on row one and under-build on row three. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. The all-rounders: chat assistants This is where nearly everyone starts, and for most people one good assistant covers 70% of what they'd otherwise buy five tools for. The honest truth in 2026 is that the top models are close enough that habit and integration matter more than benchmarks . Pick one, learn it properly, and you'll beat someone who hops between four. pages.t: A Still Place — Sit for a Moment
pages.h: A still place — sit for a moment
pages.d: A still page. A seated Buddha at dawn, a verse from the Pali Canon that changes each time you come, and a slow breath to follow. Stay as long as you like.
pages.b: A Still Place — Sit for a Moment A still place — sit for a moment As a deep lake is clear and still, so the wise grow calm on hearing the teaching. Dhammapada 82 Another verse The figure and the light around him swell and settle to pace your breathing: breathe in for four seconds as they grow, and out for six as they settle. It repeats until you leave. Breathe in Why this page exists The rest of this site is compilers, packet captures and security write-ups. This one is not. It is here because a page can be a quiet room, and quiet rooms are in short supply. Every verse shown here is from the Pali Canon, with its citation attached. That matters more than it might seem: a great many sayings passed around as the Buddha’s were never his. “Holding on to anger is like grasping a hot coal”, “what you think, you become”, “peace comes from within” — all modern inventions. If a line is worth sitting with, it is worth being honest about where it came from. There are 684 verses here, drawn from ten collections — among them the Dhammapada, the Udāna and Itivuttaka, the Sutta Nipāta, the verses of the senior monks and nuns, and the Saṁyutta Nikāya. You are unlikely to meet the same one twice in a sitting. About 279 of these translations are by Bhikkhu Sujato , published by SuttaCentral and dedicated to the public domain under CC0 ; the verses of the senior monks and nuns were translated by Bhikkhu Sujato and Jessica Walton. Thanks are owed to them, and to SuttaCentral for making the canon freely reusable. The remaining 405, an older set, came from several translators whose names were not recorded at the time — each is cited to chapter and verse and can be checked, but if you hold rights in any of them, please write to me and I will credit or replace it. pages.t: Colophon — How This Site Is Built
pages.d: How this site is built: hand-written HTML, zero dependencies, and a deploy that checks its own output. Every number on the page is counted at build time.
pages.b: Colophon — How This Site Is Built Colophon How this site is built A colophon is the note at the back of a book saying how it was made — the typeface, the paper, the press. This is that note for this site: what it runs on, what it deliberately does without, and why. Every number on this page is counted at deploy time rather than typed, so none of it can quietly go out of date. By the numbers What is actually here 183 HTML pages 62 browser labs 66 games 25 articles 0 dependencies 166 scripts, all mine 165 commits Counted on 2026-08-28 . The stack Hand-written HTML, and very little else There is no framework here, no bundler and no build step in the usual sense. Every page is an .html file you could open in a text editor, and the file you see in the repository is the file the browser is served. package.json exists to name two scripts and a Node version floor; it has 0 dependencies , and nothing generated is committed. That is a constraint rather than a boast. A site that outlives its framework is a site you can still change in five years, and most of what a framework buys you at this size is a rebuild you have to keep working. Runs on Static HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript. Vercel for hosting, with clean URLs and security headers set in vercel.json . Does without No framework, no bundler, no CSS preprocessor, no npm packages, and no cookie banner. Three measurement scripts run, all named in the privacy policy : one Google Analytics tag, Vercel Speed Insights, which times how fast the page rendered, and Vercel Web Analytics, which counts pageviews. Neither Vercel script sets a cookie. Runs in your browser The labs execute real language runtimes on WebAssembly locally, and nothing you type or drop into them is uploaded. The handful that look something up on the internet — DNS, RDAP, certificate transparency, breach and email-security checks — say so on the page and ask before they send anything. The privacy policy lists which, and to whom. The deploy A build that is allowed to say no Pushing to main runs one script in a throwaway container. It strips the comments out of the stylesheets, rewrites the sitemap dates from git history, and rebuilds the search index from the pages so a deploy can never serve a stale one. Then it checks its own output before it is allowed to succeed: critical files present and above a size floor, the ordered list of CSS selectors unchanged, braces balanced, and the page count above a floor. pages.t: aafire — The ASCII Fire Effect, Free In Your Browser
pages.d: The aalib fire demo in a terminal grid. A heat buffer, one averaging pass a frame, and a ramp of characters. Wind and intensity controls, no score.
pages.b: aafire — The ASCII Fire Effect, Free In Your Browser aafire The fire demo from aalib, the library that draws pictures out of characters. Worth knowing: nothing in it rises. Every cell is the average of the cells below it minus a small decay, run once a frame, and the flame is that arithmetic plus ten characters put in the right order. One averaging pass per frame Ten characters, ordered by ink Wind is a weight, not a shift No score, no clock Flame height 0 rows Screen alight 0% Wind Strong left Left Still Right Strong right Intensity Embers Fire Inferno Pause Restart ⛶ The aafire playfield. The game draws here once it starts. New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume This one is 78 columns wide — turn your phone sideways and it gets a great deal easier to read. Nothing to do. The two dropdowns are the whole of the controls. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data How the fire is made One pass, upward Two rows of random heat sit below the bottom of the screen. Every frame each cell takes the average of the three cells below it and the one below those, then loses a small random amount. Heat climbs exactly one row per pass and thins as it goes, and that is the whole simulation — no particles, no velocities, no flames as objects. The ramp does the rest The buffer is a field of numbers between nought and one. What makes it read as fire is the ten characters it is mapped onto, ordered by how much of a cell they fill: a full stop, a colon, up through x and S to a hash and a dollar sign. Shuffle that list and the same numbers stop looking like anything at all. Wind is a weight Leaning the fire by sampling an offset column snaps to whole cells, so a light breeze and a gale come out the same. Here the three samples from the row below are weighted 1+w, 1 and 1-w instead. They still sum to four, so the pass stays a true average and the wind moves heat sideways without creating or destroying any. The bed is not re-rolled The source rows keep their values, and only about a quarter of their cells get a new one each frame. Randomise all of them every frame and the averaging smooths the result into a flat orange band; letting hot spots persist for a few frames is what gives them time to climb into tongues. Questions people ask Is this the real aafire? No. It is the same effect written from scratch for a browser. The original is a C program driving aalib, but the arithmetic is the same idea and the character ramp is chosen the same way. Why does the flame sto Is this the real aafire? Why does the flame stop short of the top? Is there anything to do? No. It is the same effect written from scratch for a browser. The original is a C program driving aalib, but the arithmetic is the same idea and the character ramp is chosen the same way. The decay. Each row up costs a fixed slice of heat, so the fire runs out at a predictable height. Inferno lowers the decay far enough that it reaches the ceiling. Change the wind and watch it lean. That is it, which is why this is filed under toys rather than games.
