pages.d: A joke CAPTCHA that gets less reasonable with every screen and lets you through anyway, then explains what the real ones actually measure.
pages.b: Are You A Robot? — A Joke CAPTCHA That Always Lets You In Are you a robot? Tick the box, pick out the traffic lights, and carry on until the instructions stop making sense. Every screen lets you through, including the ones you get wrong, which is the joke and also roughly how the real thing works now. The last screen drops the act and says what a modern check is really reading. Eight screens, all of which you pass No images load — nothing is fetched Nothing is stored, scored or sent Works with a keyboard and a screen reader Stage 1/8 Verdict Pending Skip to the point Pause Restart ⛶ New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume Tab Move to the squares and between them Enter Select a square, or verify Click Choose a square Tap the squares, then tap Verify. Nothing here needs a keyboard. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data What the squares are actually for The puzzles lost the arms race Distorted text died because software got better at reading it than people were — Google said in 2014, when it introduced the tick box, that its own recogniser handled the hardest variants with better than 99% accuracy. Traffic lights and crossings were the replacement, and machine vision has caught up with those too. The hard ones now stop tired humans more reliably than they stop scripts. The modern ones score you, not your answer reCAPTCHA v3 shows no puzzle at all. It returns a number between 0.0 and 1.0 and leaves the site to decide what to do with it; Cloudflare Turnstile works much the same way. What they weigh is how the pointer moved, how the typing was timed, what the browser looks like, which cookies you already had and what your address has been doing lately. A grid of squares appears mostly when that score is borderline, or because somebody wanted the visitor to see a check happening. You were also doing unpaid work The original reCAPTCHA showed you two words: one it knew, one that optical character recognition had failed on while digitising scanned books and newspaper archives. Your answer to the second was the product. Later it moved to Street View house numbers, then to labelling images. The test was training the very thing it was meant to be testing for. And the cost lands on the wrong people Image grids are hard or impossible with a screen reader, the audio alternative is worse, and low vision, dyslexia and slow connections all make it harder again. So do shared addresses and VPNs, which draw more challenges. The people who get shown the most s Can I fail it? Does it record anything about me? Are the pictures real photographs? Could this be used as a real CAPTCHA? Why do real ones keep getting harder? No. Every screen accepts every answer, including no answer at all. That is the point being made rather than a shortcut — a fail state would teach the opposite of what the last screen says. It counts your pointer moves, your clicks and the seconds you spent, in variables in your own tab, so the last screen can show you the one signal a real check would care about. The numbers are shown once and are gone when you reload. Nothing is stored and nothing is sent. No, they are labelled boxes. Nothing loads over the network on this page. It also means a screen reader can read the challenge out, which real image grids manage badly if at all. No, and it would stop nothing. A script would clear all eight screens in milliseconds, which is roughly the situation genuine puzzle-based checks are in as well. Because it is an arms race with a scoreboard only one side reads. Each time recognition software catches up, the puzzle gets more awkward, and the awkwardness is felt by people rather than by the software. That is why the newest systems gave up on puzzles and went to scoring behaviour instead.

pages.t: Arithmetic — The BSD Drill, Ninety Seconds Of Mental Sums
pages.d: Ninety seconds of mental sums, from the BSD games drill. Four operations to pick from, and the numbers you get wrong keep coming back until you can do them.
pages.b: Arithmetic — The BSD Drill, Ninety Seconds Of Mental Sums Arithmetic The drill that shipped with BSD, with a ninety-second clock on it. Add, subtract, multiply and divide — pick which of those you want — and answer as many as you can. The interesting part is what happens when you get one wrong: both numbers go back into the bag, so the sums that beat you are the ones you see most. Ninety seconds Four operations, selectable Wrong numbers come back Six levels, it picks one Score 0 Best 0 Right 0 Wrong 0 Avg — Operations Addition Add & subtract Add, subtract, multiply All four Pause Restart ⛶ The Arithmetic playfield. The game draws here once it starts. New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume This one is 60 columns wide — turn your phone sideways and it gets a great deal easier to read. 0-9 Type the answer Enter Submit it Backspace Fix a digit Esc End the run early Tap the panel to bring up the number pad, then type the answer and press enter. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data How it decides what to ask you The numbers you miss go back in the bag Get a sum wrong and both of its operands are pushed onto a small pool that later questions draw from, roughly two times in five. That is the original's adaptation and it is the only part of the game that teaches anything — if you cannot do seven eights, you will be asked about sevens and eights until you can. The level moves on speed, not just accuracy Three right in a row, each answered inside eight seconds, raises the ceiling on how big the numbers get; two wrong in a row lowers it. Correct but slow holds it where it is, which is deliberate — getting there eventually is not the same as knowing it. Every division comes out whole The divisor and the answer are drawn first and multiplied to get the dividend, so there is never a remainder to argue about. Drawing two numbers at random and asking for one over the other is the usual shortcut, and it either needs a rounding rule or throws most of what it generates away. Questions people ask Can I turn off division? Yes. The dropdown picks addition only, addition and subtraction, those plus multiplication, or all four. It takes effect on the next question rather than the next run. Are the answers ever negative? No. Subtraction swaps the operands if it needs to, so the answer is always zero or more and you only ever type digits. What is the score made of? Each sum is worth its level plus a weight for the operation — one for addition, four for division. Can I turn off division? Are the answers ever negative? What is the score made of? pages.t: asciijump — Play Free Online, No Ads
pages.d: The Linux terminal game asciijump, rebuilt for the browser. Tuck down the in-run, hit the takeoff window, and hold the lean in the air. No install, no ads.
pages.b: asciijump — Play Free Online, No Ads asciijump Peter Marschall wrote asciijump for a terminal in 2003 and its whole trick is one instant. You tuck the in-run, you leave the lip, and the tenth of a second around that edge decides whether you land at forty metres or ninety. Everything after it is you trying not to spoil it. One instant decides it Three jumps a run Real ski-jump scoring Runs at 72 columns Score 0 Best 0 km/h 0 Metres 0.0 Jump 1/3 Pause Restart ⛶ The asciijump playfield. The game draws here once it starts. New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume This one is 72 columns wide — turn your phone sideways and it gets a great deal easier to read. Space Hold to tuck, let go at the lip ← → Hold the lean steady in the air Esc Pause Hold the Action button all the way down the in-run and lift your thumb at the lip. Left and right hold the lean while you are in the air. ◀ ▶ Action Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data Why the takeoff is the whole thing The window is time, not distance The game keeps a running estimate of how long until the lip — the metres of ramp left, divided by your speed — and grades your press against it. A window measured in columns instead would be wider at 70 km/h than at 100, which quietly pays you for a slow in-run. It also runs both sides of the edge, because pressing late has to be possible: otherwise holding until the ramp simply ends is free, and everybody does that instead of playing. It tells you how wrong you were Every jump ends with the miss in seconds — 0.14 s early, 0.03 s late. That number is the whole teaching mechanism. A timing game that reports only the outcome is a slot machine; one that reports the error is something you are visibly better at after ten jumps. Pressing early does not launch you early You leave the ramp when the ramp ends, not when you press. Firing early only means your legs finished extending before the edge arrived, so there is nothing left to spring with — which is why the takeoff is a multiplier on the launch rather than an event of its own. Mashing the button near the lip commits you to the first press that lands inside the window, usually about a second too soon. Distance is only half the score The scoring is the real one: sixty points at the K-point, two points a metre either side of it, and three judges marking out of twenty for how still you held the flight. A fall caps every judge at ten, so a long jump you cannot stand up is worth less than a shorter one you can. Que Is this the real asciijump? When exactly should I let go? What are the arrow keys for? Does the wind matter? Does it work on a phone? It is a rebuild, not the original binary. Same three phases, same screenful of characters, written in JavaScript so it runs in a browser tab instead of needing a terminal and a package manager. At the red lip post, and about a twentieth of a second either side of it still counts as perfect. The results panel tells you which way you missed, which is faster to learn from than any advice here. The air is unstable. Your lean drifts, and drifting further makes it drift faster, so left and right are a constant small correction rather than a steering wheel. The bar along the bottom shows where you are against where the judges want you. A headwind is airspeed and airspeed is lift, so it is worth a few metres either way. It is deliberately small: something you notice, not something that decides a jump your takeoff already decided. Yes, in landscape. Hold the Action button down the in-run and lift your thumb at the lip; left and right hold the lean once you are in the air.

pages.t: Assembly Puzzles — Write Assembly In Your Browser, Free
pages.d: Write programs for a tiny virtual machine with four registers and fifteen instructions. Eight problems, each checked against every test case and scored on size.
pages.b: Assembly Puzzles — Write Assembly In Your Browser, Free Assembly puzzles A machine with four registers, thirty-two memory cells and fifteen instructions, and eight problems to solve on it — from copying a number to reversing a list. Your program is run against every test case, not just the one on screen, and the score is the instructions you wrote plus every cycle the machine spent. Shorter programs and tighter loops both count. Fifteen instructions Four registers, 32 cells Eight levels Every test case checked Level 1/8 Cost 0 Best — Level 1. Copy a value 2. Add two numbers 3. The larger of two 4. Sum a list 5. Count down 6. Multiply without MUL 7. Largest in a list 8. Reverse a list Run Step Check Pause Restart ⛶ New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume Type Write the program Step One instruction at a time Run Watch the chosen test case Check Run every test case Tap the program box to bring up the keyboard; Run, Step and Check are in the toolbar above it. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data What the machine will and will not do The score counts two different things Cost is the number of instructions you wrote plus every cycle the machine executed across all the test cases. Counting only length would reward a clever one-liner that loops ten thousand times; counting only cycles would reward unrolling the whole thing by hand. Counting both is roughly the trade every real compiler is making. Par is shown against each level, and it is measured by running a reference solution in this same machine rather than written down. The flag behaves the way real flags do CMP a, b sets the flag to a minus b, but so do ADD, SUB, MUL, INC and DEC, from their own result. That is why DEC R0 followed by JNE loop is a complete countdown with no compare in it — the same reason the equivalent pair is the commonest loop on x86. MOV, IN and OUT leave the flag alone. Why level six takes MUL away Early processors had no multiplier at all, and multiplying meant a loop of additions — which is why multiplication cost tens of cycles when addition cost one. Doing it by hand once makes the cost model of a CPU much less abstract. Real hardware does better than repeated addition by shifting and adding, roughly one step per bit rather than one per unit. This is not a real instruction set There is no stack, no CALL or RET, no addressing beyond a register holding an address, and no overflow behaviour to speak of — a value too large for the machine is treated as your mistake r Is this x86, ARM or MIPS? Why does it say "still running after 20000 instructions"? Can I have more than four registers? Are my programs saved? Is a lower score better? None of them. It is invented, and deliberately small, so the whole instruction set fits on one screen. The register-and-flag model is closest to x86 in spirit. A loop with no way out. Usually the counter is being tested before it is decremented, or the jump goes back above the instruction that changes it. No, and that is most of the difficulty from level seven onwards. Memory is the answer: 32 cells, addressed as [6] or as [R1] when the address is in a register. They are kept in this browser only, per level, and nothing is sent anywhere. Restart clears your progress but leaves the code; clearing site data removes both. Yes. Cost is the one number where less is better, so your best is the lowest total you have posted on this device.

pages.d: Free browser Asteroids drawn as vector outlines. The ship keeps its speed when you stop thrusting, which is the whole difficulty of the game.
pages.b: Asteroids — Play Free Online, No Ads Asteroids Turn, thrust, fire. Thrust adds to the speed you already had rather than replacing it, so the ship carries on drifting long after you let go — and that one fact is the entire difficulty of the game. Every rock breaks into two smaller rocks twice before it is gone, so a full board gets busier before it gets quieter. Thrust adds, never steers Everything wraps Rocks split twice A saucer that aims Score 0 Best 0 Lives 3 Wave 1 Pause Restart ⛶ The Asteroids playfield. The game draws here once it starts. New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume ← → Turn ↑ Thrust ↓ Hyperspace Space Fire Esc Pause The D-pad turns and thrusts, down jumps to hyperspace, and Action fires. A tap anywhere on the playfield fires as well. ▲ ◀ ▶ ▼ Action Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data Why the ship is hard to fly Thrust adds to your velocity, it does not set it Holding up does not point the ship where it is going — it adds a push in the direction you are facing to the speed you already had. Let go and nothing stops you; there is only a light drag that bleeds a little off each second. So the direction you are aiming and the direction you are travelling are two separate things, and every burn has to be paid back with an opposite one later. That is the whole game, and it is why turning to face a rock is easy and getting away from it is not. The board is a torus, not a box Everything wraps, which makes a rock at the left edge and a shot at the right edge eighteen units apart rather than six hundred. Every distance in the file folds each axis into the nearer half of the board before measuring, so shots do not pass through rocks sitting on the seam. Anything close to an edge is also painted a second time on the far side, so a rock is visibly half on each edge while it crosses instead of appearing to teleport. Four shots on screen, and a range limit You can only have four of your own shots alive at once, and each one expires after about three quarters of a board width. Both limits are from the original and both are load-bearing: without them you can hold the fire button and clear a wave without aiming, and the small saucer stops being a threat worth a thousand points. Questions people ask Why does the ship keep moving after I stop thrusting? Because that is the game. There are no brakes. The only way to slow down is to turn around and thrust the other way, and the drag is deliberately light so that most of the speed you build

Spending the arrows on compass points instead would have left nothing for altitude, and altitude is half the game. Separation is judged after everyone has moved The collision test runs once, when every aircraft has taken its step for that sweep. Run it inside the movement loop instead and the aircraft early in the list are measured against positions the rest have not taken yet, so the same two either crash or do not depending on the order they happened to arrive in. That is the kind of bug a player experiences as the game cheating. Landing is a timing problem, not a button Altitude changes one level per sweep and the aircraft moves one square in the same sweep, so a descent has to be started exactly as many squares out as the altitude you are at. Reach zero anywhere except the airport square, on the runway heading, and it is a crash. None of the landing is a keypress at the right instant; all of it is arithmetic done three or four sweeps early. Questions people ask How do I get an aircraft off the radar? pages.t: Bastet — Bastard Tetris, The Evil Tetris
pages.d: Bastet — "bastard Tetris" — replaces the random piece bag with a solver that hands you the worst piece every single time. Free, in your browser.
pages.b: Bastet — Bastard Tetris, The Evil Tetris Bastet Federico Poloni’s bastet does one thing differently from Tetris, and it is enough to change the game entirely: instead of dealing pieces at random, it works out which of the seven shapes would hurt you most, and gives you that one. Every time. There is no bad luck here, only intent. The generator is a solver Every piece is your worst Same rules as Tetris otherwise 280 drops simulated per piece Score 0 Best 0 Lines 0 Level 1 Pause Restart ⛶ The Bastet playfield. The game draws here once it starts. New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume ← → Move ↑ Rotate ↓ Soft drop Space Hard drop Pad to move and rotate. Tap the board to hard-drop. ↻ ◀ ▶ ▼ Drop Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data How it decides what to give you It plays your move for you first For each of the seven shapes it drops every rotation into every column, scores the board that results, and keeps the BEST outcome — because that is what a competent player would find. Then it serves whichever shape’s best outcome is worst. That is 280 simulated drops per piece, which costs nothing and is genuinely adversarial rather than merely unlucky. Play it next to the fair one The Tetris here uses a proper 7-bag: all seven shapes shuffled and dealt, so your worst drought is capped at twelve pieces. Same rules, opposite generators. Playing both is the fastest way to understand that “random” is a design decision rather than a default, and how much of a game lives in it. Questions people ask Is it actually impossible? No. It is very hard. The solver models a decent player rather than a perfect one, and a shape with nowhere at all to go is skipped rather than served — an instant unavoidable loss reads as a broken game, not a cruel one. How is this different from just bad luck? Bad luck is a distribution. This is a search: it evaluates your actual board before choosing. pages.t: Birthday Facts — The Day You Were Born, And Every Day Since
pages.d: Enter a date of birth and get the weekday it fell on, your exact age, days alive, your next birthday and your age on seven planets. Nothing is uploaded.
pages.b: Birthday Facts — The Day You Were Born, And Every Day Since Birthday facts Type in a date of birth and this works out the day of the week it fell on, how old you are to the day, and how many days that adds up to. The weekday comes from Zeller’s congruence rather than a table somebody typed up, and every other figure is arithmetic you could check by hand. The date stays in this tab and is not saved anywhere. Weekday from Zeller’s congruence Leap years handled properly Seven planets, real orbital periods Nothing uploaded, nothing saved Born on — Days alive — Pause Restart ⛶ New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume Enter Work it out Tap the field to open your phone’s own date picker, then tap Work it out. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data The arithmetic, since that is the whole page The weekday is calculated, not looked up Zeller’s congruence turns a date into a day of the week with a few lines of integer arithmetic. It works by treating January and February as months 13 and 14 of the previous year, which moves the leap day to the end of the year and out of the middle of the sum. The same formula produces the weekday for your next birthday and for the 1,000-day marks, so all the dates on the page agree with each other by construction. Days are counted between UTC midnights Ask a browser for the gap between two local dates and you are asking about a lifetime that may contain a hundred clock changes, each an hour that has to land somewhere. Counting from UTC midnight to UTC midnight avoids the question entirely: those are exactly 86,400 seconds apart, always, so the day count is a subtraction rather than an estimate. “Years, months and days” has to pick a convention Whole months are counted first and the leftover days measured from there, with the month step clamped to the end of a short month — so one month after 31 January is 28 February and the day count restarts on the 28th. Other calculators borrow days from the previous month instead and can differ from this by a day or two around month ends. Neither is wrong; they are answering slightly different questions. The heartbeat figure is a multiplication Days alive, times 24, times 60, times 70. Seventy is the middle of the resting range for an adult and it is the only assumption in the sum. Your real rate ran far higher through childhood and changes every minute of every day, so the number is worth an order of magnitude and nothing more precise than that. Ages on other planets are just di Is the day of the week right for old dates? What if I was born on 29 February? Another calculator gives a different age. Which is right? Is my date of birth sent anywhere? How accurate is the heartbeat number? Why is Pluto not in the table? Back to 1583 it is, on the Gregorian calendar. Earlier than that the form refuses, because the Gregorian calendar arrived in 1582 in some countries, 1752 in Britain and its colonies and 1918 in Russia — so the weekday for a date in 1650 depends on where you are asking about, and one answer would be a guess dressed as a fact. Your age and day counts are exact either way, since they never need an anniversary. For the next birthday in an ordinary year this page uses 1 March; some places use 28 February instead. The result says which it used. Both, probably. The disagreement will be in the months-and-days part, near the end of a short month, and it comes from how each one adds a month to the 29th, 30th or 31st. Total days alive is not a matter of opinion and should match exactly. No. It is typed into a field, used for arithmetic in the same tab, and never leaves it. It is not stored either — no localStorage, no cookie. Reload the page and the field is empty. It is arithmetic, not measurement: days alive times 1,440 minutes times 70 beats. Treat it as the right size rather than the right number. It has not been a planet since 2006. If you want the figure anyway, its orbit is about 90,560 Earth days, so divide your days alive by that.

pages.t: Boids — Flocking Simulation You Can Break, Free In Your Browser
pages.d: Craig Reynolds's flocking model. Separation, alignment and cohesion — three rules per bird, no leader, no plan. Move the sliders and watch the flock fall apart.
pages.b: Boids — Flocking Simulation You Can Break, Free In Your Browser Boids Every bird looks only at its neighbours and follows three rules: do not crowd them, head roughly the way they are heading, and drift toward the middle of them. Nothing knows about the flock — and yet there it is. Turn one rule down and watch what it was holding together. Three rules, no leader Sliders that break it Your cursor is a hawk Hundreds of birds at sixty frames Birds 220 Separation Alignment Cohesion Flock size 80 birds 220 birds 450 birds ∿ Pause Restart ⛶ The Boids playfield. The sliders change the three rules. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data How it stays fast Neighbours by bucket, not by brute force Comparing every bird with every other is 200,000 distance checks a frame at 450 birds. Instead each bird is filed into a grid cell the size of its view radius, so it only ever looks at nine cells. That is the difference between sixty frames a second and nine. The colour is the heading Each bird is tinted by the direction it is flying, so the structure of the flock reads as colour as well as position. A flock rotating around a common centre becomes obvious instantly, which it is not when everything is one colour. Questions people ask What happens if I turn separation off? They collapse into a single point and stay there. Separation is the only rule pushing outward, so without it cohesion wins completely. And alignment? You get a milling swarm rather than a flock — they stay together but never agree on a direction. It looks like insects instead of birds. Is this how real flocks work? Broadly, yes. Reynolds proposed it in 1986 as a model rather than a measurement, and later studies of actual starlings found birds do track a small fixed number of neighbours rather than everything they can see. pages.b: Flappy — Play Free Online, No Ads Flappy One button, and a bird that is always falling. The whole game is the relationship between four numbers — how hard gravity pulls, how much a flap gives back, how fast the pipes arrive and how far apart the gaps sit — and this one is tuned so that ten gaps is a matter of rhythm rather than luck. One button, nothing else Tuned so ten gaps is rhythm The gap narrows as you score Your best kept on this device Score 0 Best 0 Gap 168 Pause Restart ⛶ The Flappy playfield. Action Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data The tuning is the game Four numbers that are really one A flap sets your upward speed rather than adding to it, so every flap draws the same 60-unit arc and takes about a third of a second to reach the top of it. Flap again as it comes back down and you hover; flap faster and you climb at roughly 190 units a second. Pipes arrive every 1.43 seconds, so you can climb about 270 units between one gap and the next — and that number is what decides how far apart consecutive gaps are allowed to be. Gap centres step, they do not jump Each gap centre is drawn as a step from the previous one, capped at 110 units. Picking every centre independently is the usual shortcut, and it produces the pair nobody can make: one gap near the ground, the next near the roof, with a second and a half to cross the lot. Capping the step well under what the flap arc can reach keeps every pair reachable without perfect timing. The ceiling does not kill you Hitting the roof takes your climb away and drops you; only the ground and the pipes end a run. Each row says in one line what that encoding is and where you would really meet it. None of them is encryption, and the page says so before it says anything else. An encoding has no key at all — it is only a different way of writing the same characters, and reversing it is a one-click operation that the encoder in the Labs section will happily do for you. Binary, Base64 and ROT13 get mistaken for security constantly, usually by somebody who has just Base64-ed a password into a config file. All that hides it from is a casual glance. Characters and bytes are different counts The two numbers in the bar disagree the moment you leave ASCII. A plain Latin letter is one byte in UTF-8, an accented one is two, most Devanagari characters are three and an emoji is four. That is why a form with a 20-character limit sometimes rejects a name that is plainly shorter than twenty letters: somebody counted bytes and called them characters. Every row is somewhere real Hex is what a memory dump or a hex editor shows you. Base64 is how an image gets into an email or a data: URL. Morse is a telegraph code with no lower case, so anything it cannot carry is dropped and the line under it says how many. ROT13 was a Usenet convention for hiding spoilers. Leetspeak matters because password crackers have known the letter-to-digit swaps for thirty years — changing e to 3 buys you nothing. Questions people ask Is what I type sent anywhere? An emoji sits far outside ASCII, so it needs all four, even though it is a single character and a single code point. Morse only defines codes for A to Z, the digits and a handful of punctuation marks. There is no Morse for an emoji, an accented letter or a non-Latin script, so those characters are left out and counted underneath rather than quietly mangled. pages.b: Personality Test — A Short Big Five Inventory, Free Personality test The one companies put in front of you at interview is almost always a five-factor inventory, not a four-letter type. This is a short version of the real thing: thirty statements, five traits, and a result that tells you where you sit rather than which fictional box you belong in. Big Five, not sixteen types Thirty items, half reverse-keyed Results as bars Nothing is uploaded Progress 1/30 Pause Restart ⛶ New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume ↑ ↓ Move between answers Space Choose Tap an answer to move on. Back returns to the previous question. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data Why this and not the four letters The type indicators do not hold up The famous four-letter one is enormously fun and has very little predictive validity: a large share of people get a different type on a retest a few weeks later, and its dichotomies are not actually bimodal in the data — most people sit in the middle, which is the one answer it cannot give. Half the questions are backwards Fifteen of the thirty are worded the opposite way and scored in reverse. Without them, anybody who agrees with everything produces the same profile as somebody thinking hard, and what you would be measuring is politeness rather than personality. Two traits, not one, decide your description The write-up blends your highest and second-highest readings, because a person who is organised and curious is nothing like a person who is organised and conventional, and a result keyed only to the top trait cannot tell them apart. It says what it is not Thirty items is short. Scores move with mood, with how recently you slept, and with whether you are answering as you are or as you would like to be. Good for reflection, not for deciding anything about anybody — and the page says so under the result rather than in the small print. Questions people ask Is this scientifically valid? The model is — the five-factor structure is the most replicated finding in personality psychology. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data How the ripples are drawn A ripple is a centre and a number The obvious way to animate a spreading ring is to keep the cells it has lit and age them. That costs memory per ripple and per cell, and where two ripples overlap you then have to decide which one owns the cell as they fade. Here a ripple is a position and a radius, the radius grows with time, and the cells are derived from it fresh on every frame by walking the angle. A round ring is an ellipse in cells A character cell here is 8 units wide and 16 tall. Plot an honest circle in cell coordinates and it arrives on screen as a tall oval. Every vertical offset is halved, so the ring is an ellipse in the grid and a circle to look at. The glyph comes from the tangent At the left and right edges of a ring the curve runs vertically, so those cells get │. At the top and bottom it runs flat, so they get ─. Fading in four steps A terminal has no alpha channel, so the fade is four colour bands — white, cyan, blue, then dim — with the leading edge always one band brighter than the two rings trailing it. Regular expressions that have to survive input you have not seen are a different job, and usually a longer one. Why a pattern can be refused Two guards. pages.t: Stack Buffer Overflow Visualiser
pages.h: Stack buffer overflow, byte by byte
pages.d: Copy a string into a fixed buffer and watch it overwrite the saved frame pointer and return address byte by byte. Then try a stack canary, NX and ASLR.
pages.b: Stack Buffer Overflow Visualiser Stack buffer overflow, byte by byte The oldest serious bug in computing is copying more bytes into an array than it can hold. It is almost always explained in prose. Here it is drawn: a real downward-growing stack, a fixed buffer at the bottom, and a string copied into it one byte at a time — climbing straight up over the saved frame pointer and into the return address the CPU will jump to. Then watch a canary catch it, and see exactly what each modern defence does and does not stop. A real byte-addressed stack, growing down Watch the return address get overwritten Control-flow hijack, drawn not executed A stack canary catching the overflow NX and ASLR, with their honest limits Before you start This runs entirely inside your browser — the animation, the maths, all of it on your own machine. Nothing is uploaded and there is no server. Good to know Everything runs on your device Heavy work runs off the main thread where it can Nothing is uploaded or stored Why it is here Seeing it beats reading about it Works offline once the page is cached Free, permanently I understand — start Take me home ⛶ Starting the buffer overflow visualiser… if this message stays, it did not load — please tell me, and mention your browser. What an overflow actually overwrites The geometry is the whole bug The stack grows downward, so a function’s local buffer sits at the bottom of its frame — and the saved frame pointer and return address sit just above it. A string copied into the buffer is written upward, toward those saved registers, with nothing in between but the absence of a bounds check. Copy one byte too many and you are writing over the address the CPU will return to. Overwriting the return address is taking the wheel When a function finishes, RET pops the saved return address into the instruction pointer and the CPU jumps there. Overwrite those four bytes and you choose the destination. Point them back at the buffer — where the attacker’s own bytes were just copied in as “data” — and the machine executes them as code. Nothing here really runs; it is a diagram of that hijack over an array in a sandboxed tab. A canary is a tripwire, not a wall A stack canary is a known value placed between the buffer and the saved registers, checked just before the function returns. A linear overflow has to run through it to reach the return address, so the check fails and the program aborts. It does not stop the overflow — it stops the return into corrupted  Is this a real exploit? Why does the copy write upward into the return address? Do buffer overflows still matter in 2026? What actually stops these? Is anything uploaded? No. It is a diagram of one. The stack is an array of bytes at pretend addresses, the overflow is a write past the end of that array, and “jump to shellcode” moves a number that represents the instruction pointer. Nothing is compiled and nothing is executed — it could not be, running as arithmetic in a sandboxed browser tab. Because that is the real memory layout. The stack grows toward lower addresses, so a local buffer is at the lowest addresses of the frame and the saved return address is above it. A C string is laid out from low address to high, so copying into the buffer writes toward — and eventually over — the return address. Yes. They are less common in memory-safe languages, but C and C++ still run most operating systems, browsers and embedded devices, and memory-safety bugs remain among the most exploited vulnerability classes every year. The mitigations shown here are why they are harder to exploit than they were, not why they have gone away. Layered mitigations raise the cost: stack canaries, non-executable memory (NX/DEP) and address randomisation (ASLR), plus compiler and hardware features beyond this lab. The complete fix is a memory-safe language - Rust, Go, Java, Python - which makes the out-of-bounds write impossible rather than merely survivable. Why lifetimes shrank The ceiling is falling on a schedule. CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081 replaced the flat 398-day maximum with fixed steps: 200 days from March 2026, 100 from March 2027, and 47 from March 2029. The limit binds at issuance, so a certificate cut before a step can legitimately outlive it — the decoder above checks against whichever ceiling applies today rather than a single number baked into the page. Shorter lifetimes limit the damage from a key compromise and force automation, which is why ACME and Let’s Encrypt became the norm. Subject Alternative Names are what browsers read The Common Name in the subject has been ignored by browsers for years. A certificate is valid for the names in its SAN extension and nothing else, which is the first place to look when a certificate that “should work” does not. What a certificate actually is A certificate is a signed statement about a key Strip away the jargon and an X.509 certificate says: “this public key belongs to this name, and I vouch for that” — signed by whoever is vouching. This lab builds that statement field by field: the subject, the validity dates, the key, the extensions, and finally the signature over all of it. Trying all of them and scoring each result against English letter frequencies takes a browser under a millisecond. Any cipher whose security depends on a small keyspace was already broken before computers existed. How Vigenère falls Index of coincidence measures how clumped the letter frequencies are: about 0.067 for English, 0.038 for random text. Split the ciphertext into n columns and the value jumps back to English levels exactly when n is the key length. Each column is then just a Caesar cipher. No guessing at any point. Single-byte XOR in the wild It is still the most common “obfuscation” in malware and CTF challenges, usually wrapped around a URL or a command string. It has 255 keys, so it is not obfuscation — it is a speed bump you clear by trying all of them. What modern ciphers had to fix Every attack here works because the ciphertext preserves statistical structure from the plaintext. AES output looks uniformly random regardless of the input, which is precisely the property that makes frequency analysis useless against it. Questions people ask Are these ciphers safe to use fo Are these ciphers safe to use for real? What is ROT13? How does it break a Vigenere cipher without the key? How much text does the automatic break need? Is my text uploaded? Absolutely not. Every one of them is broken by the buttons on this page, without a key, in milliseconds. They are here for learning, for puzzles and for CTF challenges. A Caesar cipher with a shift of 13. Because the alphabet has 26 letters, applying it twice returns the original - it is its own inverse. It was used on old forums to hide spoilers, not secrets. It finds the key length using the index of coincidence, then treats each column of the ciphertext as a separate Caesar cipher and solves each with frequency analysis. The key is derived from the ciphertext alone. Caesar needs very little. Vigenere needs at least 40 letters, and works better with more - statistical attacks need enough text for the statistics to mean anything. pages.t: Cryptography Visualiser — AES, RSA, ECC

pages.b: Cryptography Visualiser — AES, RSA, ECC Cryptography, opened up The other cryptography tools here treat the algorithm as a black box, which is exactly what a tool should do. This page is the opposite. AES becomes a grid of sixteen bytes you watch get substituted, shifted and mixed; SHA-256 becomes eight registers churning; Diffie-Hellman becomes two people arriving at the same number without ever sending it — and an eavesdropper who has to guess. AES-128 in all 40 transformations SHA-256 across every one of its 64 rounds Diffie-Hellman, RSA and ECDH with checkable numbers Checked against the NIST FIPS test vectors Step backwards as freely as forwards Before you start This runs entirely inside your browser — the animation, the maths, all of it on your own machine. What is actually happening AES is four moves, repeated Substitute every byte through the S-box, rotate the rows, mix the columns, XOR in the round key — then do it nine more times. None of the four is clever on its own; the strength comes from repetition. The avalanche chart under the state grid makes that concrete: flip one bit of the input and by round three roughly half the output bits have changed. Nothing is up anyone’s sleeve The AES S-box here is generated, not pasted — it is the multiplicative inverse in GF(2⁸) followed by an affine transform, computed when the page loads. SHA-256’s constants are the fractional parts of the square and cube roots of the first primes, also computed live. Those provenances are the argument that the designers did not hide a backdoor in a magic table, and they are far more convincing computed than asserted. Small numbers, so you can check the maths Diffie-Hellman with a 2048-bit prime is honest and completely unwatchable. With p = 23 you can follow every modular exponentiation by eye — and watch the eavesdropper break it by brute force in a couple of dozen guesses. That is the only way to feel why the real thing needs numbers with six hundred digits. This tool reverses them for you and shows the gap between each pair — a large gap means the message sat in a queue or a filter, and a negative one means the chain was forged or the clocks disagree. What SPF, DKIM and DMARC each prove SPF says the sending server was authorised to send for that domain. DKIM says the message is cryptographically signed and unmodified. DMARC says the domain owner accepts the combination. All three passing proves the message really came from that domain — not that it is honest. A lookalike domain registered yesterday passes all three too. The Reply-To mismatch A From: line showing a familiar name and a Reply-To on a different domain is the standard setup for business email compromise. The recipient sees the trusted name, and their reply goes to the attacker. This is flagged in red. Why nothing is looked up A WHOIS query, a geolocation call or a reputation check all tell a third party which address you are investigating, and in a targeted case that leaks the investigation itself. Authentication proves origin, not honesty. The ones added by servers you trust cannot, but a sender can inject fake ones before the message reaches those servers. Only the hops added after the message entered infrastructure you trust are reliable, which is why the timing checks matter. If the first hop shows a 10.x, 192.168.x or 172.16-31.x address, the message started inside a private network and the public IP appears at the next hop out.

Why one regex has three engines Two ways to run the same machine Thompson’s construction builds a state machine with at most two states per character of pattern, and the simulation tracks every state it could be in at once. That costs states times input, always. A backtracking engine instead follows one possibility at a time and rewinds when it fails — which is what makes backreferences and lookaround possible, and what makes the worst case exponential. Almost every language you use ships the second kind. ReDoS is a real denial of service Hand (a+)+ a run of a’s followed by one character it cannot match, and a backtracking engine has to prove that every way of splitting those a’s fails. pages.d: Hide a text message in the least significant bits of a PNG, extract a hidden message from an image, and amplify the low-bit layer to spot concealed data.
pages.b: Image Steganography — Hide Text in a PNG Image steganography Changing the last bit of each colour channel shifts a value by at most 1 out of 255, which no eye can see. That is why a picture can carry a paragraph and look identical — and why hiding one is the fastest way to understand finding one. JPEG destroys it. Up to 20 MB. Message Message Output Concealment is not protection How LSB works Each pixel has a red, green and blue value from 0 to 255. Replacing the last bit of each changes the colour by at most one step, which is far below what an eye or a screen can resolve. Three bits per pixel means a one-megapixel image carries about 375 KB. It survives nothing Re-save the image as JPEG, resize it, or upload it anywhere that re-encodes images, and the message is gone — because all of those rewrite exactly the bits it lives in. The result here must stay a PNG. And it is not encryption Anyone who suspects LSB reads it with the Extract button on this page. There is no key. Steganography hides the existence of a message; cryptography protects its contents. If the content matters, encrypt it before hiding it. Finding hidden data The low-bit view amplifies every least-significant bit to full brightness. Real image noise looks like static. Visible text, sharp edges, or a solid rectangle of noise in one corner means something was written there — which is exactly how this is detected in practice. pages.t: TCP Visualiser — Handshake & Congestion
pages.d: Step through the TCP handshake with real sequence numbers, walk both endpoints through the state machine, and watch Reno congestion draw its sawtooth.
pages.b: TCP Visualiser — Handshake & Congestion TCP, from handshake to sawtooth The pcap analyser elsewhere in Labs shows you TCP packets after they have flown. This lab runs the protocol. Watch the three-way handshake exchange real sequence numbers, watch both ends walk the TCP state machine to ESTABLISHED and back, and watch congestion control probe for bandwidth and back off on loss — the sawtooth that shapes very nearly every byte you have ever downloaded. The three-way handshake with real seq / ack numbers Both endpoints through the TCP state machine Reno congestion control, actually simulated Slow start, fast recovery and timeout, distinct Change the loss pattern and watch the shape respond Before you start This runs entirely inside your browser — the animation, the maths, all of it on your own machine. Nothing is uploaded and there is no server. Good to know Everything runs on your device Heavy work runs off the main thread where it can Nothing is uploaded or stored Why it is here Seeing it beats reading about it Works offline once the page is cached Free, permanently I understand — start Take me home ⛶ Starting the TCP visualiser… if this message stays, it did not load — please tell me, and mention your browser. What TCP is doing under a download The handshake is a sequence-number agreement SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK is not a greeting ritual — it is both ends agreeing on the sequence number each will start counting from, so that every byte afterwards can be ordered and acknowledged. A SYN consumes one sequence number; data advances it by its length; an acknowledgement is always “the next byte I expect from you”. The numbers on the ladder are the real arithmetic, not decoration. TIME_WAIT is the state everyone forgets Closing a connection takes four segments, not three, because each direction is shut independently. The side that closes first then sits in TIME_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime — long enough that a straggling old segment cannot be mistaken for part of a new connection reusing the same ports. It is why a busy server can accumulate thousands of sockets in TIME_WAIT, and why that is normal rather than alarming. Congestion control is why the internet works at all No sender knows how much bandwidth the path has, so TCP finds out by probing: start slow, double the window every round trip until something is lost, then back off and probe more gently. Because every connection does this, they share a link roughly fairly without any central coordinator Are the sequence numbers real? Which congestion-control algorithm is this? Why does the window collapse to 1 on a timeout but only halve on duplicate ACKs? Is this a real network connection? Is anything uploaded? Yes. The handshake tracks genuine seq/ack arithmetic - a SYN or FIN consumes one sequence number, data advances the sequence by its length, and each acknowledgement is the next byte expected. The test suite checks these against the worked examples in RFC 793. TCP Reno: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery. It is the classic textbook algorithm and the ancestor of what most systems still run. Modern variants like CUBIC and BBR change the growth curve, but the core idea - probe up, back off on loss - is the one shown here. Because they signal different things. Duplicate ACKs mean packets are still arriving, so the path is working and a gentle cut is enough. A timeout means the sender has heard nothing back, so it must assume the pipe has drained and start probing from scratch. That asymmetry is deliberate and is the shape of the sawtooth. No. It is a simulation of the protocol running as arithmetic in your browser. Nothing is sent, no socket is opened, and the only real TCP involved is the one that delivered this page. Change the inputs and the simulation recomputes; that is all it is doing. No. Every segment and every round trip is computed locally, and there is no network request.

pages.t: Timestamp Converter — Unix & FILETIME
pages.d: Convert timestamps between Unix, Windows FILETIME, WebKit, Apple Cocoa, HFS+ and MS-DOS epochs at once, and identify what produced an unknown value.
pages.b: Timestamp Converter — Unix & FILETIME Forensic timestamp converter A registry key gives you a FILETIME, a browser history database gives you WebKit microseconds, a macOS plist gives you seconds since 2001. They are all “a number”, and reading one with the wrong epoch puts your event in 1601. So this reads it under all of them. Unix, FILETIME, WebKit, Cocoa, HFS+ MS-DOS packed ZIP timestamps Flags which readings are plausible Works in both directions Nothing uploaded Before you start This tool runs entirely inside your browser. Nothing you paste or drop here is uploaded, logged or stored — which for security work is the whole point, not a footnote. What it does not do No uploads — there is no server to upload to No account, no history, nothing saved Conversions use UTC unless a zone is given Local time is shown using your device clock Why that matters here Evidence files stay on your machine A token or key you paste is never transmitted Nothing you paste ever appears in your Network tab Works with no internet once the page is cached Free, permanently I understand — open the tool Take me home Now ▶ Convert ⛶ Timestamp Timestamp Output Why there are so many epochs Every platform picked its own zero Unix counts seconds from 1970. Windows counts 100-nanosecond ticks from 1601, because that is the start of the Gregorian 400-year cycle. Apple counts from 2001 in Cocoa and from 1904 in HFS+. None of them are wrong; they just do not interoperate. Where you meet each one FILETIME comes out of the registry, NTFS MFT records and Windows event logs. WebKit microseconds come out of Chrome’s History, Cookies and Login Data databases. Cocoa comes out of macOS and iOS plists. Getting these wrong puts an event centuries away from where it belongs, which is a common and embarrassing timeline error. The identification trick Because the epochs are so far apart, reading one number under all of them almost always leaves exactly one answer in a believable date range. That single plausible reading tells you which system wrote it, without knowing anything else about the source. The number of seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC, ignoring leap seconds. It is the most common timestamp format in logs, APIs and JWT exp claims. The number of 100-nanosecond intervals since 1 January 1601 UTC. It appears in the registry, NTFS metadata and Windows event logs, and the values are very large - around 133 quadrillion for a recent date. Paste it here. pages.b: Krunalkumar Shah Research | Publications & Ideas Research interests Exploring ideas that connect technology, security, and thoughtful innovation. Research remains central to my work, whether it is publishing academic material or applying fresh thinking to cybersecurity and practical systems. Publication Security Against Fork Bomb Attack in Linux Based Systems Krunalkumar D. Shah & Krunal V. Patel · International Journal of Research in Advent Technology (IJRAT), Vol. 7, No. 4, April 2019 · E-ISSN 2321-9637 · DOI: 10.32622/ijrat.74201911 🏅 Nominated for the Best Paper Award in Linux research at IAENG The problem I set out to solve A fork bomb is a denial-of-service attack in which a process endlessly replicates itself until the process table and memory are exhausted, freezing the system. What drew me to it is that creating a process is a legitimate operation needing no special privileges, so even hardened Linux systems are vulnerable — availability, one of the three pillars of information security, breaks down. Why the existing defenses weren’t enough Static process limits reject legitimate work once the cap is hit. Rate limits misfire on fork-heavy software such as CAD tools. Name-based blacklists never forgive: a legitimate process that shares a name with a past offender is killed forever. Each approach trades one failure mode for another, and that is the gap I set out to close. The defense I proposed I combined name-based detection with something I call process resource quarantine. New processes are monitored for their fork rate; offenders are killed and their name recorded. When a recorded name reappears, I do not kill it outright — it runs inside a resource quarantine and is inspected. If it behaves, it is released and removed from the list, so a false positive corrects itself instead of lasting forever. What my results showed I evaluated the system with a bash fork bomb on Xubuntu 18.04 (kernel 4.15). It identified an attack in as little as 44 ms at a threshold of 500 forks, while known offenders were handled instantly by name — and the machine stayed responsive and available throughout, which was the whole point. The paper, narrated, in a hundred seconds: a fork bomb filling the process table until the machine stops answering, then the same attack run against the defense. pages.b: Terms of Service Terms Terms of Service Plain-language ground rules for using this site and working with me. Individual projects usually get their own written scope — where one exists, it takes precedence over these terms. Effective date: 5 August 2026 · Applies to krunalkumar.dpdns.org What these terms cover These terms apply to your use of this website and to services provided by Krunalkumar Shah, an independent consultant based in Gujarat, India — including automation and AI workflows, software development, security reviews, corporate and team training, personal cyber help, research collaboration, and the internship and mentorship programs . The business is registered with the Ministry of Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises (MSME), Government of India — Udyam Registration No. UDYAM-GJ-23-0050928. By using the site or engaging any of these services, you agree to these terms. The rules I work by Authorized access only. I work only on devices, accounts, and systems that you own or are explicitly authorized to grant access to. I may ask for proof of ownership, and I will decline or stop any work where that isn't clear. No exceptions. Honest certificates. Internship certificates describe the real project work an intern shipped; mentorship certificates state that the mentorship program was completed. Neither claims employment or titles that didn't happen. Confidentiality. Anything you share with me for an engagement — code, data, credentials you authorize, business details — is used only for that engagement and is not shared with anyone else. Payments and refunds Fees are agreed in writing before work begins. The paid mentorship is billed month to month at the price published on the Internships page , and you can cancel anytime. Refunds are handled as described in the Refund Policy . What you can expect — and what I can't promise I bring professional skill and honest effort to every engagement, and I tell you plainly when something is outside my expertise. What I cannot promise are specific outcomes: no security review makes a system unbreachable, no mentorship guarantees a job offer, and no automation is immune to changes in the third-party services it depends on. Where an outcome can't be delivered, the Refund Policy says what happens next. Intellectual property Deliverables created for a client belong to the client once the agreed fee is paid, unless the project's written scope says otherwise. pages.t: Certificate Verification
pages.d: Verify the authenticity of an internship or mentorship completion certificate issued by Krunalkumar Shah. Enter the certificate ID to see the official record.
pages.b: Certificate Verification Certificate verification Verify a certificate. Every completion certificate I issue carries a unique certificate ID, printed on the document next to a QR code. Enter that ID below to see the official record. If a certificate’s details do not match what this page shows, treat the record here as the authoritative one. If an ID is not found at all, email me and I will confirm it directly — a missing record is not by itself proof that a certificate is not genuine. Check a certificate Enter the certificate ID and hit Verify Try it now with the sample ID KS-INT-2026-SAMPLE to see how a verified record looks. Certificate ID Verify For colleges & employers How to use this page Match the paper Compare the name, work description, dates, and status shown here with the document in front of you. A genuine document matches its record exactly. Scan or type — same result The QR code on the document opens this page with the ID pre-filled. Typing the address yourself and entering the ID by hand returns the same record. Need a human? For institutional verification queries, email krunalkumar@krunalkumar.dpdns.org — I answer verification requests personally.
